title: "Final Critical-Count Calibration in Single-Arm Binary Promising-Zone Designs"
subtitle: "An Exact-Enumeration Study of Adaptation Mappings and Final Decision Rules"

abstract: |
  Promising-zone sample size re-estimation (SSR) is often paired with
  a one-sided one-proportion z-test final analysis in single-arm
  binary trials, by analogy with the Mehta-Pocock construction for
  continuous endpoints. We evaluate this extension by exact enumeration
  using conditional power under the observed interim response rate. In one
  oncology configuration, the fixed-sample z-test has 5.80% Type I error;
  conditional-power designs across the promising-zone grid have 5.55%-5.69%.
  Changing only the fixed-sample final rule shifts the attained level by 2.32
  percentage points, whereas the re-estimation mapping changes it by at most
  0.12 points across one-look timings from 40%-77% information. In two
  representative two-look schedules, the mapping contribution is at most
  0.21 points, versus at least 1.41 points for the score-z versus exact-final
  contrast. The uncorrected score-z critical count is never larger than the
  exact-binomial count over reachable sample sizes, identifying normal
  approximation as the operative mechanism. Exact-binomial finals control
  Type I error at 3.42%-3.89%, with a 3.79-6.40-point power cost;
  inverse-normal combination tests using exact stagewise p-values also
  control at 3.32%-3.54%, while a mid-p variant reaches 5.52%. Designers
  should prespecify the final decision rule and report exact operating
  characteristics for the complete adaptive design.

# Introduction

Single-arm Phase II oncology trials with a binary objective response
rate (ORR) endpoint are a long-standing design framework for assessing
biological activity of investigational agents [@simon1989]. In this
setting, the trial sponsor must commit to a sample
size before observing data on the new agent, and yet the assumed effect
size, and therefore the planned power, is rarely well-calibrated. Sample
size re-estimation (SSR) addresses this by allowing the planned $N$ to be
adjusted at an interim analysis based on observed information.

Among adaptive SSR strategies, the **conditional-power promising zone**
framework developed in the Chen--DeMets--Lan and Mehta--Pocock work is a
prominent, practically implemented approach to unblinded SSR
[@chen2004; @mehta2011; @edwards2020]. Its appeal is partly statistical and
partly regulatory.
For the conventional final Wald statistic, Mehta and Pocock build on the
Chen--DeMets--Lan result that Type I error is not inflated when sample-size
increases are restricted to a sufficiently high conditional-power zone
[@chen2004; @mehta2011]. Separately, the inverse-normal combination test of
@lehmacher1999 and the equivalent weighted statistic of @cui1999 provide an
analytic guarantee under more general data-dependent sample-size changes by
retaining design-fixed weights. The 2019 FDA adaptive design guidance [@fda2019]
explicitly recognises this design family and states that Type I error
control should be demonstrated, analytically where possible, otherwise via
simulation.

A practical question is how this framework transfers to single-arm binary
endpoints. Both the interim statistic and the final rejection region are
functions of integer response counts. A conventional one-proportion
$z$-test therefore induces a design-specific integer critical count whose
attained Type I error need not equal its nominal level. The combination-test
principle itself does transfer: valid stagewise binomial $p$-values can be
combined with weights fixed at the design stage. What does not transfer
is calibration of the final $z$-test critical count, which is already
inexact at the planned sample size and is not repaired by the adaptation.

We study a representative oncology design with $p_0=0.23$, $p_1=0.35$,
one-sided $\alpha=0.05$, $N_0=84$, $n_1=65$, and $N_{\max}=200$. The
final test is the null-variance score-form $z$ statistic without continuity
correction. Conditional power is calculated under the response rate
estimated at interim, as in the Mehta-Pocock promising-zone construction,
and the sample size is increased until conditional power reaches its upper
target or the cap is reached. Exact enumeration shows that the fixed-sample test already has
`r percent(headline_fixed_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error; across the
prespecified promising-zone grid the adaptive design ranges from
`r percent(min(headline_cp_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(headline_cp_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`. Thus adaptation is not
the primary cause of inflation in this setting.

We compare fixed-$N$, conditional-power (CP), and Bayesian
predictive-probability (PP) adaptation mappings under $z$ and posterior
final rules. Within-mapping final-rule contrasts and fixed-$N$ references
keep adaptation and final-decision effects distinct. We also
evaluate coherent joint boundary-and-mapping calibration, remove futility stopping,
repeat both designs across alternative parameter settings, verify the
least-favorable null, and construct exact and mid-$p$ inverse-normal
combination tests. These analyses distinguish three issues that are easy to
conflate: calibration of the final critical count, the mapping from interim
counts to sample size, and early stopping. The remainder of the paper reviews the
background, defines the comparisons, presents exact operating
characteristics, and discusses their practical implications.


# Background


## Single-Arm Phase II Design

Single-arm Phase II oncology trials test the response rate $p$ of a new
agent against a historical null $p_0$ [@simon1989]. Simon's two-stage
design fixes both stage sizes and permits early termination. Subsequent
work developed flexible and adaptive extensions for binary single-arm
trials, including designs that modify second-stage enrollment or optimize
the design after the first stage [@lin2004; @banerjee2006; @shan2016].

Bayesian alternatives operate on the posterior $P(p > p_0 \mid x, n)$
under a Beta-Binomial model. @lee2008 proposed a predictive-probability
design for Phase II cancer trials in which the trial monitors the posterior
probability that it will *eventually* declare success at the planned final
analysis. The predictive probability under a Beta($a, b$) prior and
binomial likelihood is available in closed form as a Beta-Binomial sum
[@lee2008; @saville2014].

The choice between conditional power (CP) and predictive probability (PP)
for interim monitoring has been debated since at least @spiegelhalter1986.
CP evaluates the chance of eventual rejection under a specified projection
for the remaining observations; in the Mehta-Pocock promising-zone rule,
that projection uses the treatment effect estimated at interim
[@mehta2011]. PP instead averages over the posterior distribution of $p$;
the two are formally related, and @lan2009 expresses predictive power as an
average of conditional power over that posterior. For a Beta-Binomial
model, PP is available as a finite sum and is therefore natural to monitor
in single-arm binary trials [@lee2008; @saville2014].


## Sample Size Re-estimation

@mehta2011 developed the practical **conditional-power promising zone**
framework for SSR, extending the conditional-power result of @chen2004. At an
interim analysis, CP is computed using the observed treatment-effect
estimate. Three thresholds, futility ($\text{CP}_\text{fut}$), promising
lower ($\text{CP}_L$), and promising upper ($\text{CP}_U$), partition
the CP scale into futility, unfavorable, promising, and favorable zones.
In the promising zone the planned $N$ is increased to a value chosen so
that CP at the new $N$ rises to $\text{CP}_U$ (capped at a budget
$N_\text{max}$). The justification for retaining the conventional final
statistic is the Chen--DeMets--Lan promising-zone result: sample size may be
increased without inflating Type I error when the interim estimated-effect
conditional power is above a safe lower bound [@chen2004; @mehta2011]. This
is distinct from the more general combination-test route. The inverse-normal
test of @lehmacher1999 and the equivalent weighted statistic of @cui1999
combine pre- and post-interim statistics with design-fixed weights that are
invariant to the SSR decision; the conditional rejection probability
principle of @muller2001 provides another general route. The fixed-weight
invariance yields analytic Type I error control without relying on the
promising-zone restriction.

@dmitrienko2006 presented a Bayesian predictive approach to interim
monitoring, following the earlier conditional-versus-predictive-power
formulation of @spiegelhalter1986. Predictive monitoring was later developed
and applied in single-arm Phase II and broader interim-monitoring contexts by
@lee2008 and @saville2014;
@liu2023 subsequently studied predictive-power-based SSR specifically
for Phase 2 dose-finding. We adopt this lineage's PP design here. The PP design uses two independent thresholds: an *interim
efficacy* bar $\gamma_\text{int}$ (stop early for success if
$P(p > p_0 \mid x_\text{int}, n_\text{int}) \geq \gamma_\text{int}$)
and a *final analysis* bar $\gamma_\text{final}$ (declare success at
the end of the trial if $P(p > p_0 \mid x_\text{total}, n_\text{final})
\geq \gamma_\text{final}$). The predictive probability used as the
interim SSR trigger is computed *under* $\gamma_\text{final}$, not
$\gamma_\text{int}$. Because the final success count changes only at
discrete threshold values, Type I error is a step function of
$\gamma_\text{final}$ rather than a continuous one; in every setting
evaluated here it is also decreasing, though monotonicity does not follow
from discreteness alone. Exact enumeration
can nevertheless identify threshold-specific rejection regions that
control Type I error.

The inverse-normal argument also has a binary analogue. Let $P_1$ be a valid
one-sided binomial $p$-value from stage 1 and let $P_2$ be conditionally
super-uniform given the stage-1 data and the resulting prespecified choice
of stage-2 sample size. For $w_1^2+w_2^2=1$, with both weights fixed before
adaptation, the statistic
$w_1\Phi^{-1}(1-P_1)+w_2\Phi^{-1}(1-P_2)$ is stochastically no larger under
the null than the corresponding statistic based on independent uniform
$p$-values. It therefore yields a valid, generally conservative,
combination test [@lehmacher1999; @cui1999]. We quantify that conservatism
and compare it with a mid-$p$ version, which is less conservative but lacks
the same finite-sample guarantee [@lancaster1961].


# Methods


## Design Parameters

We consider a single-arm Phase II oncology trial with a binary objective
response rate (ORR) endpoint, comparing the response rate $p$ against a
historical null $p_0$,

$$H_0: p \leq p_0 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_1: p = p_1 .$$

An interim analysis is conducted at $n_\text{int}$ patients. Depending
on the observed data, the trial either stops early (efficacy or futility)
or continues, with the option to extend enrollment up to a budget cap
$N_\text{max}$. The base-case design parameters reflect a representative
single-arm Phase II oncology setting. The base case is $p_0 =
`r p0`$, $p_1 = `r p1`$, one-sided $\alpha = `r alpha`$, planned
$N_\text{init} = `r n_init`$, interim at $n_\text{int} = `r n_int`$,
budget cap $N_\text{max} = `r n_max`$, promising-zone bounds
$\text{CP}_\text{fut} = `r cp_futility`$ and $\text{CP}_U =
`r cp_upper`$, interim efficacy bar $\gamma_\text{int} = `r gamma_int`$,
and a Jeffreys $\text{Beta}(`r ap`, `r bp`)$ prior. These values are
defined once, in `R/params.R`, which both this article and the
supplementary material source, so the two cannot report different
settings.

```{r params}

stopifnot(

  exists("n_max"), exists("gamma_fin_cal"), exists("PRIMARY_CP_MODE")
)
```


## Final Decision Rules

For a total sample size $N$, the frequentist final analysis uses

$$Z_N=\frac{X_N/N-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/N}}.$$

This is the null-variance score-form statistic, evaluated against
$z_{1-\alpha}$ without continuity correction. Its integer critical count is

$$c_z(N,\alpha)=\left\lfloor Np_0+z_{1-\alpha}
\sqrt{Np_0(1-p_0)}\right\rfloor+1.$$

The exact null rejection probability is therefore
$P_{p_0}\{X_N\geq c_z(N,\alpha)\}$, which need not equal $\alpha$.
The exact binomial comparator instead rejects at

$$c_e(N,\alpha)=\min\left\{x:
P_{p_0}(X_N\geq x)\leq\alpha\right\}.$$

This rejection region, equivalently obtained by inverting a one-sided exact
binomial confidence bound, is non-anticonservative for every fixed $N$
[@clopper1934]. In the
adaptive comparison, the CP zones and selected sample sizes remain those
defined by $c_z$; only the final critical count is replaced by $c_e$. This
holds the adaptation mapping fixed and isolates the final-rule effect.
The Bayesian final rule uses a Jeffreys Beta$(0.5,0.5)$ prior and declares
success when $P(p>p_0\mid X_N,N)\geq\gamma_\mathrm{final}$.

A fourth rule is carried through the comparisons as a diagnostic rather
than as a design proposal. Applying the usual continuity correction to the
score statistic gives

$$c_{z,\mathrm{cc}}(N,\alpha)=\left\lfloor Np_0+z_{1-\alpha}
\sqrt{Np_0(1-p_0)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor+1,$$

which can only shift the count upward relative to $c_z$. Because the
correction addresses the normal approximation to a discrete distribution
and leaves the integer grid untouched, comparing $c_{z,\mathrm{cc}}$ with
$c_e$ separates miscalibration attributable to the approximation from
miscalibration attributable to discreteness itself. All numerical
implementations of these rules are defined in `R/analysis.R`.



## CP Promising Zone SSR

At interim sample size $n_1$, let $x_1$ responses be observed and define
$\widehat p_1=x_1/n_1$. For candidate total sample size $N$, conditional
power is calculated under the observed response-rate estimate,

$$\mathrm{CP}(x_1,n_1,N) =
P\!\left\{X_2 \geq c_z(N,\alpha)-x_1
\;\big|\; X_2 \sim \text{Bin}(N-n_1, \widehat p_1)\right\},$$

where $c_z(N,\alpha)$ is the $z$-test critical count at sample size
$N$ and the same one-sided $\alpha$ that the final analysis uses. The
primary analysis uses the raw maximum-likelihood estimate $x_1/n_1$, with
no shrinkage or bounding. At the extreme counts $x_1=0$ and $x_1=n_1$, the
remaining-response distribution is correspondingly degenerate at zero or
one, so CP remains well-defined. The trial then proceeds according to

$$
\text{Action} = \begin{cases}
\text{Futility stop} & \text{if } \text{CP} < \text{CP}_\text{fut} \\
\text{Unfavorable: continue to } N_\text{init} & \text{if } \text{CP}_\text{fut} \leq \text{CP} < \text{CP}_L \\
\text{Promising: SSR to } N' \leq N_\text{max} & \text{if } \text{CP}_L \leq \text{CP} < \text{CP}_U \\
\text{Favorable: continue to } N_\text{init} & \text{if } \text{CP} \geq \text{CP}_U
\end{cases}
$$

with $\text{CP}_U$ fixed at $0.80$ (the target power) and
$\text{CP}_\text{fut} = 0.10$ throughout. The promising-zone SSR rule
extends $N$ until CP rises back to $\text{CP}_U$, capped at
$N_\text{max}$. The final analysis is a one-sided one-proportion
$z$-test at $\alpha = 0.05$. There is no interim efficacy stop in the
CP design. The same critical count is used in the conditional-power
calculation and at the final analysis. We sweep the promising lower bound
$\text{CP}_L$ over the grid $\{0.30, 0.35, \ldots, 0.80\}$.
This grid is a sensitivity analysis, not a claim that each value satisfies
the continuous-endpoint safe-zone condition of @chen2004 and @mehta2011.
For the discrete binary design, we evaluate the attained Type I error of the
complete rule directly.



## Bayesian PP SSR

The Bayesian design uses *separate* thresholds for the interim efficacy
stop ($\gamma_\text{int}$) and the final analysis success criterion
($\gamma_\text{final}$). The SSR trigger is the predictive probability
of eventual success at the planned $N$, computed *under*
$\gamma_\text{final}$:

$$
\text{PP}(x_\text{int}, n_\text{int}, N) =
\sum_{x_r=0}^{N - n_\text{int}}
\text{BetaBin}(x_r;\; n_r,\; a_\text{post},\; b_\text{post})
\cdot \mathbf{1}\!\left[P(p > p_0 \mid x_\text{int}+x_r,\, N) \geq \gamma_\text{final}\right] .
$$

At the interim, the trial stops early for efficacy when the posterior
$P(p > p_0 \mid x_1,n_1) \geq \gamma_\text{int}$. Otherwise, it stops
for futility when $\mathrm{PP}\leq0.05$, increases the sample size when
$0.05<\mathrm{PP}<\mathrm{PP}_U$, and continues to $N_0$ without an
increase when $\mathrm{PP}\geq\mathrm{PP}_U$, with $\mathrm{PP}_U=0.50$
in the base design. In the increase zone, the smallest $N\leq N_{\max}$
that raises PP to $\mathrm{PP}_U$ is selected; if no such value exists,
$N_{\max}$ is used. The upper boundary marks the point at which eventual
success is at least as likely as failure under the predictive distribution.

Two structural asymmetries with the conditional-power design should be
noted, because they affect what the two can be asked to reveal when
compared. First, the predictive-probability design has **no
unfavorable-continue region**: every interim outcome above the futility
boundary and below $\mathrm{PP}_U$ triggers an increase, whereas the
conditional-power design routes outcomes below $\text{CP}_L$ to
$N_\text{init}$ without adaptation. The predictive-probability design therefore has no
unfavorable-continue region, and at a comparable threshold it adapts on
more null mass than the conditional-power design; the two adapting sets
are not nested, however, so neither contains the other. Second, the conditional-power design has no interim efficacy
stop, while this one does; where the two are compared directly in
@sec-factorial the efficacy stop is disabled so that the contrast reflects
the final rule rather than an extra early-rejection opportunity. Because this
choice is operational rather than error-controlling, we also assess upper
boundaries from 0.30 to 0.70. We fix $\gamma_\text{int}=0.99$; a value of
0.95 would itself yield
`r percent(1 - pbinom(x_crit_fn(n_int, p0, ap, bp, 0.95) - 1L, n_int, p0), accuracy = 0.01)`
null rejection at $n_1=65$ before the SSR branch is evaluated.
We prespecify a sweep of $\gamma_\text{final}$ over
$\{0.950, 0.955, \ldots, 0.990\}$ and select the smallest grid value whose
exact null rejection probability does not exceed $\alpha$. This rule is
available prospectively because it uses only the prespecified design and
exact enumeration under $p=p_0$; it selects $`r gamma_fin_cal`$ in the
base design. The
final analysis declares success when the posterior at $n_\text{final}$
reaches or exceeds $\gamma_\text{final}$.


## Repeated-Look Sensitivity Design

The repeated-look sensitivity uses CP schedules at 40% and 65% information
($n=34,55$) and at 50% and 77% ($n=42,65$). Let $N^{(j)}$ be the current
sample-size target at look $j$, with $N^{(0)}=N_\text{init}$. At each look,
CP is evaluated against the score-$z$ critical count at $N^{(j)}$. A futility
result stops the trial; an unfavorable or favorable result retains
$N^{(j)}$; and a promising result selects the smallest
$N\in\{N^{(j)},\ldots,N_\text{max}\}$ attaining $\text{CP}_U$. Thus a later
look may increase but never reverse an earlier increase. There is no interim
efficacy rejection. Exact operating characteristics enumerate the first-look
count, the increment to the second look, and the final increment. The
exact-final contrast freezes every pathwise target selected by this score-$z$
CP rule and replaces only the final critical count.




## Exact Operating Characteristics

Because the primary designs have a single interim look and a binomial
endpoint, every operating characteristic, Type I error, power, expected
sample size, zone probabilities, sample-size quantiles, is **exactly
computable** by enumerating the joint distribution of
$(x_\text{int},x_\text{rem})$ under any true response rate $p$. The compact
two-look sensitivity is likewise evaluated exactly by pathwise recursion.
Every reported operating characteristic is therefore deterministic and has
no Monte Carlo error. The one-look implementation is centralized in
`R/analysis.R`, and the repeated-look recursion is in
`R/two_look_sensitivity.R`; simulation remains available for extensions
where enumeration becomes impractical.

Six true ORR scenarios are evaluated: $p_0$, three intermediate values
($p_0 + 0.25\Delta$, $p_0 + 0.50\Delta$, $p_0 + 0.75\Delta$ with
$\Delta = p_1 - p_0$), $p_1$, and an over-performing arm
$p_1 + 0.25\Delta$. For each design we report power (or Type I error
when $p = p_0$), expected sample size $E[N]$, zone probabilities,
budget-cap probability, and the $p10$/$p50$/$p90$ quantiles of
$n_\text{final}$. Generalizability is assessed by repeating the
CP $\text{CP}_L$ sweep across five distinct $(p_0, p_1, n_\text{int},
N_\text{init}, N_\text{max})$ settings. All code is in R 4.x with
Quarto; the manuscript is fully reproducible from this `.qmd`. Practice-
oriented sensitivities additionally evaluate a coherently specified
continuity-corrected score design, a 0.001 posterior-threshold grid,
departures of the actual untreated response rate from the historical
benchmark, and exact bias and naive 95% interval coverage after adaptation.
A seeded Monte Carlo run provides a stochastic cross-check of the primary
exact calculations.
Separately, `R/independent_validation.R` reimplements the base design in base
R without sourcing the manuscript engine or parameter file and reproduces six
selected fixed and adaptive operating characteristics.
No method is optimized under a common power, expected-sample-size, or maximum-
sample-size constraint. Cross-method power and efficiency differences are
therefore comparisons of the prespecified operating points, not rankings of
the best achievable versions of the methods.


# Results


## CP Promising Zone: Attained Level Relative to the Fixed-$N$ Reference

Exact Type I error (T1E) at $p = p_0$ sits above the nominal
$\alpha = 0.05$ at every $\text{CP}_L$ from $0.30$ to $0.80$, varying
only mildly across the grid (@fig-cp-t1e). Read against $\alpha$ alone
this looks like an adaptation effect. It is not. The fixed-$N$ score-$z$
test at $N_\text{init}$, with no interim analysis and no re-estimation,
already attains
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * headline_fixed_t1e)`. **Every adaptive value on
the grid lies below that reference**, so relative to its own
no-adaptation counterpart the design is attenuating, not inflating. The
excess over $\alpha$ is inherited from the final decision rule before any
adaptation occurs.

Two features of the base design govern how much the adaptation *could*
move the attained level. The interim sits at
$n_\text{int} / N_\text{init} =$
`r sprintf("%.2f", headline_info_frac)` of the planned sample size, later
than the roughly one-half information fraction typical of the
Mehta--Pocock construction. Consequently, under $H_0$,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * headline_pr_fut)` of trials stop for futility,
and at most
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * headline_pr_prom[2])`
of null mass ever reaches the promising zone, falling to zero at
$\text{CP}_L = 0.80$ where no interim count is classified as promising.
The futility probability does not depend on $\text{CP}_L$, since the
futility boundary is held fixed throughout.
The re-estimation therefore acts on at most a handful of interim counts,
and the small size of its effect in this setting is partly a property of
interim timing rather than of promising-zone SSR in general.
@sec-factorial separates the contributions directly.

The variation across the grid is small but deterministic: adjacent
$\text{CP}_L$ values often map the same interim integer counts into the
same zones, so the exact T1E curve changes only in steps when an integer
crosses a zone boundary, and it is **not monotone** in $\text{CP}_L$.
No $\text{CP}_L$ on the grid achieves $\text{T1E} \leq \alpha$ while
$\text{CP}_U$, the futility boundary, and the $0.05$ final level are
held fixed. Supplementary Table S1 reports power at $p = p_1$ alongside
T1E at each $\text{CP}_L$. Section 4.2 decomposes the inherited fixed-$N$ score-$z$
bias and the signed changes produced when SSR moves trials between
integer critical counts; @fig-generalizability then shows that the
*direction* of the attained-level bias changes from one design
configuration to another, so the base-setting excess is not universal.

```{r cp-sweep}
#| cache: true
#| message: false

# Headline OC: exact enumeration (no Monte Carlo noise).
cp_sweep <- expand_grid(
  cp_lower = cp_lower_grid,
  p_true   = scenarios
) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(cp_lower, p_true) {
    cp_oc_exact(
      p_true = p_true, cp_lower = cp_lower,
      cp_upper = cp_upper, cp_futility = cp_futility,
      n_init = n_init, n_int = n_int, n_max = n_max,
      p0 = p0, p1 = p1, alpha = alpha, ap = ap, bp = bp,
      cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE
    )
  })
```

```{r fig-cp-t1e}
#| fig-cap: "Exact Type I error of the adaptive CP-$z$ design across the promising lower-bound grid, at $p_0 = 0.23$, $p_1 = 0.35$, $n_\\text{int} = 65$, $N_\\text{init} = 84$, $N_\\text{max} = 200$, $\\text{CP}_U = 0.80$ and $\\text{CP}_\\text{fut} = 0.10$, by exact enumeration. The grey dashed line is the fixed-$N$ score-$z$ test at $N_\\text{init}$ with no interim analysis and no re-estimation; the red dotted line is nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$. Every adaptive value lies below the fixed-$N$ reference, so relative to its own no-adaptation counterpart the design attenuates rather than inflates the attained level."

t1e_only <- cp_sweep |>
  filter(p_true == p0)

# Fixed-N reference: attained score-z T1E before any interim analysis or SSR.
# The adaptive curve differs through both the SSR mapping and futility stopping;
# the no-adaptation comparison in the factorial section separates them.
t1e_fixed <- fixed_n_t1e(n_init, p0, alpha)

# coord_cartesian (not scale limits) so no point can be silently dropped.
cp_rng  <- range(c(t1e_only$power, alpha, t1e_fixed))
cp_pad  <- max(diff(cp_rng) * 0.18, 1.5e-3)
cp_ylim <- c(cp_rng[1] - cp_pad, cp_rng[2] + cp_pad)
cp_span <- diff(cp_ylim)

ggplot(t1e_only, aes(x = cp_lower, y = power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, color = COL_ALPHA, linewidth = 0.6,
             linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = t1e_fixed, color = COL_FIXED, linewidth = 0.6,
             linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = COL_BLUE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = COL_BLUE, size = 3, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
  # Annotations sit above their own reference line. The two lines are only
  # ~0.8 pp apart, so the labels are placed at opposite ends of the panel to
  # keep them from colliding: alpha on the right, fixed-N on the left.
  annotate("text", x = max(cp_lower_grid), hjust = 1,
           y = ann_above(alpha, cp_span),
           label = TeX("$\\alpha = 5\\%$"),
           size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_ALPHA) +
  annotate("text", x = min(cp_lower_grid), hjust = 0,
           y = ann_above(t1e_fixed, cp_span),
           label = TeX("fixed-$N$ $z$-test"),
           size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_FIXED) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cp_lower_grid,
                     labels = as.character(cp_lower_grid)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1),
                     breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = cp_ylim) +
  labs(
    x = TeX("CP promising lower bound ($\\textrm{CP}_L$)"),
    y = TeX("Exact Type I error ($p = p_0$)")
  ) +
  fig_theme(legend = "none")
```

Supplementary Table S1 reports the full operating characteristics at four
representative $\text{CP}_L$ values. In the base setting, the excess over $\alpha$ is
small in absolute terms, typically a few tenths of a percentage point, but
it occurs at every $\text{CP}_L$ on the prespecified grid. Power at $p_1$
decreases monotonically in $\text{CP}_L$, but the attained level does not
move with it: $\text{CP}_L \in [0.35, 0.55]$ attains both a lower level and
higher power than $\text{CP}_L \in [0.60, 0.75]$ (Supplementary Table S15), so
raising $\text{CP}_L$ does not buy level control at the price of power.

```{r cp-oc-summary}
#| include: false
# Values retained in the main text after the full operating-characteristic
# table moved to the supplement.
.cp_ref  <- cp_sweep |> filter(round(cp_lower,4) == 0.50)
cp_ref_pow  <- .cp_ref |> filter(p_true == p1) |> pull(power)
cp_ref_en   <- .cp_ref |> filter(p_true == p1) |> pull(exp_n)
cp_ref_fut  <- .cp_ref |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(pr_fut)
cp_ref_prom <- .cp_ref |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(pr_prom)
cp_ref_cap  <- .cp_ref |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(pr_cap)
```

At the representative setting $\text{CP}_L = 0.50$ the design attains
`r percent(cp_ref_pow, accuracy = 0.01)` power at $p_1$ with expected sample
size `r sprintf("%.1f", cp_ref_en)`. Under $H_0$ it stops for futility with
probability `r percent(cp_ref_fut, accuracy = 0.1)`, enters the promising
zone with probability `r percent(cp_ref_prom, accuracy = 0.1)`, and reaches
the cap $N_\text{max}$ with probability
`r percent(cp_ref_cap, accuracy = 0.1)`. Operating characteristics at six
response scenarios and four $\text{CP}_L$ values, including power, expected
sample size, sample-size percentiles and full zone occupancy, are given in
Supplementary Table S1.


## Mechanism: Score-$z$ Attained-Level Bias and Boundary Crossings

```{r cp-mechanism}
# ── For each x_int, compute CP at n_init and the SSR target N ─────────────
# n_ssr(x_int) is the smallest n in [n_init, n_max] with CP(n) >= cp_upper,
# i.e., the N this integer would drive to under the SSR rule if it fell in
# the promising zone. fp_at_ssr is the resulting conditional false-positive
# probability at that N. fp_at_init is the FP probability if no SSR were
# done (integer falls in unfavorable). The signed difference governs the
# T1E contribution change when that integer crosses promising -> unfavorable.
mechanism_tbl <- tibble(x_int = 0L:n_int) |>
  mutate(
    cp_at_init  = map_dbl(
      x_int,
      ~ cp_fn(.x, n_int, n_init, p0, p1, alpha,
              cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE)
    ),
    prob_x_null = dbinom(x_int, n_int, p0),
    # Critical count under z-test, same helper used by cp_fn / sim_trial_cp
    xc_init     = x_crit_z_fn(n_init, p0, alpha),
    x_need_init = pmax(0L, xc_init - x_int),
    fp_at_init  = map2_dbl(x_int, x_need_init,
                           ~ if (.y > n_init - n_int) 0
                             else 1 - pbinom(.y - 1L, n_init - n_int, p0)),
    # SSR target N per x_int (capped at n_max if cp_upper unreachable)
    n_ssr       = map_int(x_int, function(x) {
      for (nc in seq(n_init, n_max)) {
        if (cp_fn(x, n_int, nc, p0, p1, alpha,
                  cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) >= cp_upper) return(nc)
      }
      n_max
    }),
    xc_ssr      = map_int(n_ssr, ~ x_crit_z_fn(.x, p0, alpha)),
    x_need_ssr  = pmax(0L, xc_ssr - x_int),
    fp_at_ssr   = pmap_dbl(list(x_int, x_need_ssr, n_ssr),
                           function(xi, xn, ns) {
                             nr <- ns - n_int
                             if (xn > nr) 0
                             else 1 - pbinom(xn - 1L, nr, p0)
                           }),
    # T1E contribution change as this integer crosses promising -> unfavorable
    # (loses the SSR-conditional FP, gains the no-SSR FP at n_init)
    t1e_change  = prob_x_null * (fp_at_init - fp_at_ssr)
  )

# ── For each CP_L step, identify integers that cross the boundary ─────────
# When CP_L is raised from pl_old to pl_new (pl_new > pl_old),
# integers with pl_old <= CP < pl_new move from promising → unfavorable
boundary_crossings <- map_dfr(
  seq_along(cp_lower_grid[-1]),
  function(i) {
    pl_old <- cp_lower_grid[i]
    pl_new <- cp_lower_grid[i + 1]
    mechanism_tbl |>
      filter(cp_at_init >= pl_old, cp_at_init < pl_new) |>
      mutate(
        pl_from  = pl_old,
        pl_to    = pl_new,
        step     = glue("{pl_old} -> {pl_new}")
      )
  }
)
```

```{r mechanism-crossings}
#| include: false
# Builds bc_plot, which supplies the crossing count and total magnitude
# quoted above and is exported for Supplementary Figure S2. The rendered
# figure itself moved to the supplement.

# Only plot steps that have at least one crossing
bc_plot <- boundary_crossings |>
  filter(!is.na(step)) |>
  mutate(
    delta_pp = 100 * t1e_change,
    # Two-line axis label built as a plotmath expression rather than a TeX
    # string: latex2exp does not support line breaks, but plotmath's atop()
    # stacks two rows natively. Rendered by parse(text = ...) in the y scale.
    #   row 1: x_int = <count>
    #   row 2: CP_L: <from> -> <to>
    crossing = sprintf(
      "atop(x[plain(int)] == %d, plain(CP)[L] * ':' ~ %.2f %%->%% %.2f)",
      x_int, pl_from, pl_to
    ),
    crossing = forcats::fct_reorder(crossing, delta_pp)
  )

```

Three sources determine the pattern, in descending order of magnitude.
First, the nominal score-$z$ threshold maps to a design-specific integer
critical count and therefore an attained fixed-$N$ level that can lie above
or below $\alpha$. It is above $\alpha$ in the base setting, whereas
@fig-generalizability includes settings in which it is below. Second,
futility removes null trials before the final analysis. Third and smallest,
SSR moves surviving trials among finite-$N$ tests with different attained
levels. Supplementary Table S13 quantifies the futility contribution, and
Supplementary Figure S2 gives the individual SSR boundary crossings.

The dominant source is a property of the uncorrected score-$z$
approximation, not discreteness itself. All four final rules considered here
reduce to integer critical counts. The exact binomial rule selects its count
to keep the attained level at or below $\alpha$; the uncorrected score-$z$
rule solves a normal-approximation equation and frequently selects a smaller
count. The continuity correction closes most of this gap.

Raising $\text{CP}_L$ reclassifies only interim counts whose conditional
power crosses the new boundary. For a reclassified count, the signed change
from extending the trial to retaining $N_\text{init}$ is

$$
\Delta\text{T1E}(x_\text{int})
= \Pr(x_\text{int} \mid p_0)
\cdot \bigl[\text{FP}_\text{init}(x_\text{int})
- \text{FP}_\text{ssr}(x_\text{int})\bigr],
$$

where $\text{FP}_\text{init}$ and $\text{FP}_\text{ssr}$ are the conditional
false-positive probabilities at the two targets. The sign can go either
way. Only `r nrow(bc_plot)` interim counts cross a boundary on the evaluated
grid; their total absolute contribution is
`r sprintf("%.2f", sum(abs(bc_plot$delta_pp)))` percentage points. This
explains the small nonmonotone variation in CP Type I error without making
the boundary-crossing effect the primary mechanism.

```{r crit-count-setup}
#| cache: true

# Critical counts under all four final rules across the realized range of N.
# Every design in this paper rejects iff x_total >= crit, so two rules sharing
# a critical count at a given N ARE the same test at that N. This table is the
# direct evidence for the paper's central claim.
crit_n_show <- c(n_int, n_init, 100L, 120L, 150L, n_max)
crit_show <- crit_count_table(crit_n_show, p0 = p0, alpha = alpha,
                              ap = ap, bp = bp, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_cal)

# Full realized range, for the summary statistics quoted in prose.
crit_full <- crit_count_table(seq.int(n_int, n_max), p0 = p0, alpha = alpha,
                              ap = ap, bp = bp, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_cal)
crit_wide <- crit_full |>
  select(n, rule, crit) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = crit)

n_all_agree   <- crit_wide |>
  filter(z == z_cc, z == exact, z == posterior) |> pull(n)
n_z_below_e   <- sum(crit_wide$z <  crit_wide$exact)
n_z_above_e   <- sum(crit_wide$z >  crit_wide$exact)
n_total_grid  <- nrow(crit_wide)
lvl_exceed <- crit_full |>
  group_by(rule) |>
  summarise(frac_above = mean(t1e > alpha), max_lvl = max(t1e), .groups = "drop")

# Compare the posterior and exact-binomial rules over the candidate range and
# over sample sizes actually reached by the calibrated PP mapping.
post_eq_exact_n <- sum(crit_wide$posterior == crit_wide$exact)
post_ne_exact <- crit_wide |>
  filter(posterior != exact)
pp_mapping_cal <- bayes_pp_mapping(
  gamma_fin_cal, gamma_int, pp_fut, pp_upper,
  n_init, n_int, n_max, p0, ap, bp
)
# Final-rule differences matter only on paths that continue past the interim;
# futility and efficacy stops at n_int are already terminal decisions.
pp_reached_n <- pp_mapping_cal |>
  filter(zone %in% c(1L, 2L)) |>
  pull(n_final) |>
  unique() |>
  sort()
post_ne_exact_reached <- post_ne_exact |>
  filter(n %in% pp_reached_n)

pp_post_t1e <- bayes_oc_exact(
  p0, gamma_fin_cal, gamma_int, pp_fut, pp_upper,
  n_init, n_int, n_max, p0, ap, bp
)$power
pp_exact_t1e <- bayes_oc_exact_final(
  p0, gamma_fin_cal, gamma_int, pp_fut, pp_upper,
  n_init, n_int, n_max, p0, alpha, ap, bp
)$power
pp_post_power <- bayes_oc_exact(
  p1, gamma_fin_cal, gamma_int, pp_fut, pp_upper,
  n_init, n_int, n_max, p0, ap, bp
)$power
pp_exact_power <- bayes_oc_exact_final(
  p1, gamma_fin_cal, gamma_int, pp_fut, pp_upper,
  n_init, n_int, n_max, p0, alpha, ap, bp
)$power
```

The uncorrected score-$z$ rule is not merely one discrete rule among
several. Across the realized range $N \in [`r n_int`, `r n_max`]$ its
integer critical count is **strictly below** the exact-binomial count at
`r n_z_below_e` of `r n_total_grid` sample sizes and **never above it**
(`r n_z_above_e` of `r n_total_grid`). A uniformly smaller critical count
is a uniformly larger rejection region, which is precisely why its
attained level exceeds $\alpha$ at
`r percent(lvl_exceed$frac_above[lvl_exceed$rule == "z"], accuracy = 1)`
of sample sizes while the exact rule never does. The continuity-corrected
$z$ agrees with the exact count almost everywhere, which localises the
problem to the approximation rather than to the integer grid.

```{r tbl-crit-count}
#| tbl-cap: "Integer critical count under each final decision rule, with the attained fixed-$N$ Type I error. Every design considered here rejects when $x_\\text{total} \\geq c$, so rules sharing a critical count at a given $N$ are the same test at that $N$. The uncorrected score-$z$ count is never larger than the exact-binomial count, and is often smaller; the continuity-corrected $z$, the exact binomial, and the posterior rule agree far more often with each other than any of them does with the uncorrected $z$."

crit_show |>
  mutate(cell = paste0(crit, " (", percent(t1e, accuracy = 0.01), ")")) |>
  select(n, rule, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = cell) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    n           = md("$N$"),
    z           = md("score $z$"),
    z_cc        = md("score $z$, cc"),
    exact       = md("exact binomial"),
    posterior   = md("posterior")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(md(glue(
    "Each cell gives the critical count with the attained level in ",
    "parentheses. Nominal $\\alpha = {alpha}$; posterior rule at ",
    "$\\gamma_\\text{{final}} = {gamma_fin_cal}$; ",
    "cc = continuity-corrected."
  ))) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), table.font.size = "small",
              heading.title.font.size = "small",
              heading.subtitle.font.size = "footnotesize")
```

At the planned sample size $N_\text{init} = `r n_init`$ the uncorrected
$z$ rule rejects at
`r crit_wide$z[crit_wide$n == n_init]` responses while all three
alternatives require
`r crit_wide$exact[crit_wide$n == n_init]`. That single-count difference
is the whole of the base-setting excess over $\alpha$.

Agreement between the rules is common but not systematic. All four share a
critical count at
`r length(n_all_agree)` of `r n_total_grid` sample sizes in the realized
range, and within the six sample sizes displayed in @tbl-crit-count only
$N = `r if (120 %in% n_all_agree) 120 else min(n_all_agree)`$ does so. Where
they agree they are, at that $N$, the same test; where they differ the
score-$z$ rule is the one with the larger rejection region. The practical
consequence is that a design cannot be judged by whichever rule happens to
coincide at its planned sample size: the relevant comparison is over the
range of $N$ the adaptation can actually reach.

The posterior and exact-binomial rules agree often, but they are not
equivalent. They share a critical count at `r post_eq_exact_n` of
`r nrow(crit_wide)` candidate sample sizes and differ at
`r nrow(post_ne_exact)`. The calibrated PP mapping reaches
`r paste(pp_reached_n, collapse = ", ")`; at
`r paste(post_ne_exact_reached$n, collapse = " and ")` of these the
posterior critical count is one response lower than the exact-binomial
count. Holding
that PP mapping and its interim decisions fixed, the posterior final has
`r percent(pp_post_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error and
`r percent(pp_post_power, accuracy = 0.01)` power, whereas replacing only
the final boundary by the exact-binomial rule gives
`r percent(pp_exact_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` and
`r percent(pp_exact_power, accuracy = 0.01)`. Bayesian control in this
example therefore comes from prospective calibration of the complete PP
design, not from reproducing the exact test.




## Bayesian PP SSR: Monotone Type I Error Calibration

@fig-bayes-t1e shows the Bayesian counterpart of the CP
analysis, with full operating characteristics in Supplementary Table S2.
Exact Type I error decreases monotonically as $\gamma_\text{final}$
increases, in steps, because each threshold maps to an integer final
critical count. Enumeration can therefore identify the smallest
prespecified $\gamma_\text{final}$ whose complete design does not exceed
the Type I error budget, although exact equality with $\alpha$ is not
generally attainable.

Power is **not** monotone in $\gamma_\text{final}$. Because predictive
probability is evaluated against the final posterior threshold, raising
$\gamma_\text{final}$ both lifts the final critical count, which lowers
power, and enlarges the sample size the promising zone targets, which
raises it. Over the evaluated grid the second effect dominates at several
steps, so power rises slightly even as Type I error falls. The monotonicity
that makes prospective threshold selection possible is a property of the
Type I error curve alone.

This is therefore a coherent joint recalibration of the final rule and the
PP mapping, not a frozen-mapping final-rule contrast; @sec-factorial
supplies the latter.

```{r bayes-sweep}
#| cache: true

# Headline OC: exact enumeration (no Monte Carlo noise).
bayes_sweep <- expand_grid(
  gamma_fin = gamma_fin_grid,
  p_true    = scenarios
) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(gamma_fin, p_true) {
    bayes_oc_exact(
      p_true = p_true, gamma_fin = gamma_fin, gamma_int = gamma_int,
      pp_fut = pp_fut, pp_upper = pp_upper,
      n_init = n_init, n_int = n_int, n_max = n_max,
      p0 = p0, ap = ap, bp = bp
    )
  })
```

```{r fig-bayes-t1e}
#| fig-cap: "Bayesian predictive-probability SSR operating characteristics: exact Type I error at $p_0$ (left) and exact power at $p_1$ (right), as functions of the final posterior threshold $\\gamma_\\text{final}$. The red dotted line is nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$; the grey dotted line in the right panel is the 80% power target. The grey long-dashed vertical line in both panels marks the selected threshold. Both curves are step functions because each threshold maps to an integer final critical count. The panels use separate vertical scales."

# Data-driven limits. Hard-coded limits silently clip the series when the
# swept range changes: at gamma_final >= 0.975 exact T1E falls below 3%, which
# the previous ylim = c(0.03, 0.07) cut off entirely. pad_lims() always keeps
# the reference line (alpha, or the 80% power target) inside the panel.
pad_lims <- function(v, ref, frac = 0.08) {
  lo <- min(c(v, ref)); hi <- max(c(v, ref))
  pad <- max((hi - lo) * frac, 1e-3)
  c(lo - pad, hi + pad)
}

t1e_vals   <- bayes_sweep |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(power)
power_vals <- bayes_sweep |> filter(p_true == p1) |> pull(power)
gamma_fin_selected <- bayes_sweep |>
  filter(p_true == p0, power <= alpha) |>
  slice_min(gamma_fin, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(gamma_fin)

# The same threshold is computed early in document order (gamma_fin_cal) so
# that the Methods text and the critical-count table can refer to it before
# bayes_sweep exists. Two derivations of one quantity can drift; assert they
# agree rather than trusting that they do.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(gamma_fin_selected, gamma_fin_cal)))

# Left panel uses a fixed 1%-7% axis at 1% intervals so the stepwise
# structure is read against a regular grid rather than a data-driven one.
# The series is verified to lie inside this window before plotting.
bayes_t1e_lim <- c(0.01, 0.07)
stopifnot(min(t1e_vals) >= bayes_t1e_lim[1], max(t1e_vals) <= bayes_t1e_lim[2])
bayes_t1e_span <- diff(bayes_t1e_lim)

p_bayes_t1e <- bayes_sweep |>
  filter(p_true == p0) |>
  ggplot(aes(gamma_fin, power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, color = COL_ALPHA, linetype = "dotted",
             linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = gamma_fin_selected, color = COL_FIXED,
             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(color = COL_GOLD, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = COL_GOLD, fill = "white", shape = 21, size = 2.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(gamma_fin_grid), hjust = 1,
           y = ann_above(alpha, bayes_t1e_span),
           label = TeX("$\\alpha = 5\\%$"),
           size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_ALPHA) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     breaks = seq(0.01, 0.07, by = 0.01)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = bayes_t1e_lim) +
  labs(x = TeX("$\\gamma_{final}$"), y = "Exact Type I error") +
  fig_theme(legend = "none")

# The 80% target is a power reference, not a nominal level, so it is drawn in
# the neutral reference colour: red is reserved for alpha throughout.
power_span <- diff(pad_lims(power_vals, 0.80))

p_bayes_power <- bayes_sweep |>
  filter(p_true == p1) |>
  ggplot(aes(gamma_fin, power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, color = COL_FIXED, linetype = "dotted",
             linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = gamma_fin_selected, color = COL_FIXED,
             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(color = COL_BLUE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = COL_BLUE, fill = "white", shape = 21, size = 2.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(gamma_fin_grid), hjust = 1,
           y = ann_above(0.80, power_span),
           label = "80% power", size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_FIXED) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = pad_lims(power_vals, 0.80)) +
  labs(x = TeX("$\\gamma_{final}$"), y = "Exact power") +
  fig_theme(legend = "none")

p_bayes_t1e + p_bayes_power
```

```{r bayes-oc-summary}
#| include: false
.pp_ref <- bayes_sweep |> filter(round(gamma_fin,4) == round(gamma_fin_selected,4))
pp_ref_t1e  <- .pp_ref |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(power)
pp_ref_pow  <- .pp_ref |> filter(p_true == p1) |> pull(power)
pp_ref_en   <- .pp_ref |> filter(p_true == p1) |> pull(exp_n)
pp_ref_eff  <- .pp_ref |> filter(p_true == p0) |> pull(pr_eff)
```

At the selected $\gamma_\text{final} = `r gamma_fin_selected`$ the design has
`r percent(pp_ref_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error and
`r percent(pp_ref_pow, accuracy = 0.01)` power at $p_1$, with expected sample
size `r sprintf("%.1f", pp_ref_en)`. Under $H_0$ it stops early for efficacy
with probability `r percent(pp_ref_eff, accuracy = 0.1)` and for futility
with probability `r percent(pp_ref_fut, accuracy = 0.1)`. Operating
characteristics across the response scenarios and five $\gamma_\text{final}$
values appear in Supplementary Table S2.

## Joint Boundary-and-Mapping Calibration and Futility Sensitivity

Sweeping $\text{CP}_L$ changes the adaptation rule. Sweeping
$\gamma_\mathrm{final}$ changes both the posterior rejection boundary and
the PP mapping because predictive probability targets that boundary. The
coherent frequentist analogue fixes the promising-zone thresholds and varies
the nominal final-test level $\alpha_\mathrm{final}$; conditional power and
the SSR target are recalculated against each candidate boundary, so this too
is a joint boundary-and-mapping calibration. With
$\text{CP}_L=0.50$, lowering $\alpha_\mathrm{final}$ produces a
Type I error-controlling design. Supplementary Table S12 reports the largest
controlling value on a 0.0001 grid. Its achieved Type I error is conservative
because adjacent nominal levels can share an integer critical count. Thus
the appropriate claim is narrow: no $\text{CP}_L$ on the prespecified grid
controls Type I error when the other zone boundaries and the 0.05 final
level are held fixed.

```{r tbl-joint-calibration}
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Joint calibration of the CP design by varying the nominal final z-test level with the promising-zone thresholds fixed at $\\mathrm{CP}_L=0.50$. Conditional power and the SSR target are recomputed against each candidate final boundary, so the adaptation mapping may also change."
alpha_fin_grid <- seq(0.035, 0.055, by = 0.0001)

joint_calibration <- map_dfr(alpha_fin_grid, function(a_fin) {
  bind_rows(
    cp_oc_exact(p_true = p0, cp_lower = 0.50, alpha_fin = a_fin,
                cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |> mutate(estimand = "Type I error"),
    cp_oc_exact(p_true = p1, cp_lower = 0.50, alpha_fin = a_fin,
                cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |> mutate(estimand = "Power")
  ) |> mutate(alpha_fin = a_fin)
})

alpha_fin_cal <- joint_calibration |>
  filter(estimand == "Type I error", power <= alpha) |>
  slice_max(alpha_fin, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(alpha_fin)

joint_calibration |>
  filter(round(alpha_fin, 4) %in% round(c(0.0500, 0.0450,
                                          alpha_fin_cal, 0.0400), 4)) |>
  mutate(`Final alpha` = sprintf("%.4f", alpha_fin),
         Estimand = estimand,
         Probability = percent(power, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  select(`Final alpha`, Estimand, Probability) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Estimand, values_from = Probability) |>
  arrange(desc(`Final alpha`)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(`Final alpha` = md("$\\alpha_\\text{final}$")) |>
  tab_source_note(md(glue(
    "Largest controlling value on the grid: $\\alpha_\\mathrm{{final}} = {sprintf('%.4f', alpha_fin_cal)}$. Exact enumeration; observed-effect CP."
  ))) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels())
```

```{r tbl-no-futility}
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Exact operating characteristics with and without futility stopping. Interim efficacy remains active only for the Bayesian design."
no_fut_results <- bind_rows(
  cp_oc_exact(p0, 0.50, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
    mutate(Design = "CP + z", Futility = "Yes", estimand = "Type I error"),
  cp_oc_exact(p1, 0.50, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
    mutate(Design = "CP + z", Futility = "Yes", estimand = "Power"),
  cp_oc_exact(p0, 0.50, cp_futility = -Inf,
              cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
    mutate(Design = "CP + z", Futility = "No", estimand = "Type I error"),
  cp_oc_exact(p1, 0.50, cp_futility = -Inf,
              cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
    mutate(Design = "CP + z", Futility = "No", estimand = "Power"),
  bayes_oc_exact(p0, gamma_fin_selected) |>
    mutate(Design = "PP + posterior", Futility = "Yes", estimand = "Type I error"),
  bayes_oc_exact(p1, gamma_fin_selected) |>
    mutate(Design = "PP + posterior", Futility = "Yes", estimand = "Power"),
  bayes_oc_exact(p0, gamma_fin_selected, pp_fut = -Inf) |>
    mutate(Design = "PP + posterior", Futility = "No", estimand = "Type I error"),
  bayes_oc_exact(p1, gamma_fin_selected, pp_fut = -Inf) |>
    mutate(Design = "PP + posterior", Futility = "No", estimand = "Power")
)

no_fut_t1e <- no_fut_results |>
  filter(estimand == "Type I error") |>
  select(Design, Futility, power) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Futility, values_from = power)
cp_futility_delta <- with(no_fut_t1e |> filter(Design == "CP + z"), No - Yes)
pp_futility_delta <- with(
  no_fut_t1e |> filter(Design == "PP + posterior"), No - Yes
)

# Expected sample size is reported alongside: removing the futility branch
# reroutes the trials that would have stopped into the increase branch, so
# the cost of the sensitivity design is visible rather than implicit.
no_fut_en <- no_fut_results |>
  filter(estimand == "Type I error") |>
  select(Design, Futility, exp_n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Futility, values_from = exp_n)
pp_en_yes <- no_fut_en |> filter(Design == "PP + posterior") |> pull(Yes)
pp_en_no  <- no_fut_en |> filter(Design == "PP + posterior") |> pull(No)

# Build the probability and E[N] halves separately and join. Reshaping both
# at once with names_glue is fragile when a value column name contains
# brackets, so keep the two pivots explicit.
nf_prob <- no_fut_results |>
  mutate(Probability = percent(power, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  select(Design, Futility, estimand, Probability) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = estimand, values_from = Probability)

nf_en <- no_fut_results |>
  filter(estimand == "Type I error") |>
  transmute(Design, Futility, `E[N]` = round(exp_n, 1))

nf_prob |>
  left_join(nf_en, by = c("Design", "Futility")) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Design") |>
  # The whole label must sit inside math mode: "E[$N$]" puts square brackets
  # in markdown link position, so gt renders them literally instead.
  cols_label(`E[N]` = md("$E[N]$ under $p_0$")) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels())
```

Supplementary Table S13 shows that removing futility raises Type I error by
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * cp_futility_delta)` percentage points for the CP
design and by `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * pp_futility_delta)` points for the
Bayesian design in the base setting. The Bayesian result at the selected
$\gamma_\mathrm{final}$ changes from controlling to noncontrolling, so its
apparent calibration cannot be attributed to the posterior final rule alone.
The cost is visible in expected sample size, which rises from
`r sprintf("%.1f", pp_en_yes)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", pp_en_no)` under
$p_0$: outcomes that previously stopped for futility are rerouted into the
sample-size-increase branch, so the no-futility variant is a diagnostic
rather than a design anyone would run.

Comparing these magnitudes to the SSR contribution isolated in
@sec-factorial gives the ordering stated in Section 4.2. Futility moves
the attained level
by roughly a quarter of a percentage point for the CP design, whereas the
re-estimation mapping alone moves it by
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(headline_ssr_only))` to
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * max(headline_ssr_only))` points across the
$\text{CP}_L$ grid. Both are small against the
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * headline_final_rule_fixed)`-point contrast
produced by changing the final decision rule at fixed $N$, where no
adaptation is involved at all.


## Generalizability

```{r generalizability}
#| cache: true

# The base row is built from the R/params.R constants rather than retyped, so
# it cannot drift from the configuration analysed elsewhere in the article
# and keep claiming to be "(base)". The other four are deliberately different
# designs and are stated as literals.
gen_grid <- tribble(
  ~p0,  ~p1,  ~n_int, ~n_init, ~n_max, ~label,
  0.10, 0.25,  40L,    55L,    150L,   "p0=0.10, p1=0.25",
  0.20, 0.35,  50L,    72L,    180L,   "p0=0.20, p1=0.35",
  p0,   p1,   n_int,  n_init,  n_max,  sprintf("p0=%.2f, p1=%.2f (base)", p0, p1),
  0.30, 0.45,  55L,    75L,    200L,   "p0=0.30, p1=0.45",
  0.40, 0.55,  60L,    85L,    200L,   "p0=0.40, p1=0.55"
)

# Plotmath labels keep statistical subscripts out of programming notation in
# facet strips while preserving the plain labels used in tables and joins.
gen_strip_labels <- set_names(
  pmap_chr(gen_grid, function(p0, p1, n_int, n_init, n_max, label) {
    base_suffix <- if (str_detect(label, "base")) ' ~~ "(base)"' else ""
    glue('p[0] == {sprintf("%.2f", p0)} * "," ~~ ',
         'p[1] == {sprintf("%.2f", p1)}{base_suffix}')
  }),
  gen_grid$label
)

# Generalizability sweep: exact enumeration across 5 design configurations.
gen_results <- pmap_dfr(gen_grid, function(p0, p1, n_int, n_init, n_max, label) {
  map_dfr(cp_lower_grid, function(pl) {
    cp_oc_exact(
      p_true   = p0,  # T1E only
      cp_lower = pl,
      n_init   = n_init, n_int = n_int, n_max = n_max,
      p0 = p0, p1 = p1, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE
    ) |>
      mutate(scenario_label = label, p0 = p0, p1 = p1)
  })
})

# Summaries quoted in the prose below. Computed rather than typed so the
# sentences cannot drift from the figure they describe.
gen_by_setting <- gen_results |>
  group_by(scenario_label) |>
  summarise(max_t1e = max(power),
            spread  = max(power) - min(power),
            .groups = "drop")
gen_inflating   <- gen_by_setting |> filter(max_t1e >  alpha)
gen_controlling <- gen_by_setting |> filter(max_t1e <= alpha)
gen_max_spread  <- max(gen_by_setting$spread)

# The prose states that each setting is either inflating at EVERY CP_L or
# controlling at every CP_L -- i.e. that no setting straddles alpha. That is
# an empirical fact about these five designs, not a theorem, so assert it:
# if a future parameter change makes a setting straddle alpha, the render
# fails here rather than printing a sentence that is no longer true.
stopifnot(
  nrow(gen_inflating) + nrow(gen_controlling) == nrow(gen_by_setting),
  all((gen_results |> group_by(scenario_label) |>
         summarise(straddles = min(power) <= alpha & max(power) > alpha,
                   .groups = "drop"))$straddles == FALSE)
)
```

Before considering adaptation, Supplementary Table S14 compares the two final
rules at the planned sample size. This fixed-$N$ contrast isolates final
critical-count calibration because neither design has an interim look or
sample size adaptation.

To examine how CP T1E behaviour generalises beyond the base setting,
we repeat the CP $\text{CP}_L$ sweep across five
$(p_0, p_1, n_\text{int}, N_\text{init}, N_\text{max})$ combinations
spanning $p_0 \in \{0.10, 0.20, 0.23, 0.30, 0.40\}$. @fig-generalizability shows
that **CP T1E behaviour is highly design-specific**. In the base
setting ($p_0 = 0.23$) and the $p_0 = 0.20$ setting, exact T1E sits
above $\alpha = 0.05$ at every $\text{CP}_L$ on the grid. In the
$p_0 = 0.10$, $p_0 = 0.30$, and $p_0 = 0.40$ settings, exact T1E is at or
below $\alpha$ at every $\text{CP}_L$ on the grid. No setting straddles
$\alpha$: whether a design controls the level is decided by the
configuration, not by $\text{CP}_L$, which moves T1E by at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * gen_max_spread)` percentage points within a
setting.
Across these five settings, the score-$z$ critical count has an attained
level whose sign and magnitude relative to $\alpha$ depend on $(p_0,N)$,
and SSR shifts trials between finite-$N$ tests with different attained
levels. These empirical results do not support transferring a calibrated
$\text{CP}_L$ from one design to another. Each design configuration requires
its own enumeration or high-precision simulation; the five settings are not
an exhaustive characterization of the parameter space.


```{r tbl-fixed-n}
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Fixed-N comparison of the score-form z test and exact one-sided binomial test at the planned sample size, before any interim look or SSR. T1E is evaluated at p0 and power at p1."

fixed_n_comparison <- gen_grid |>
  mutate(
    z_crit = pmap_int(
      list(p0 = p0, n_init = n_init),
      function(p0, n_init) x_crit_z_fn(n_init, p0, alpha)
    ),
    exact_crit = pmap_int(
      list(n_init = n_init, p0 = p0),
      function(n_init, p0) x_crit_exact_fn(n_init, p0, alpha)
    ),
    z_t1e = pmap_dbl(list(n_init, p0),
                     function(n_init, p0) fixed_n_t1e(n_init, p0, alpha)),
    exact_t1e = pmap_dbl(list(n_init, p0),
                         function(n_init, p0) fixed_n_t1e_exact(n_init, p0, alpha)),
    z_power = pmap_dbl(list(n_init, p1, z_crit),
      function(n_init, p1, z_crit) 1 - pbinom(z_crit - 1L, n_init, p1)),
    exact_power = pmap_dbl(list(n_init, p1, exact_crit),
      function(n_init, p1, exact_crit) 1 - pbinom(exact_crit - 1L, n_init, p1))
  )

fixed_n_comparison |>
  transmute(
    Setting = glue(
      "$p_0={sprintf('%.2f', p0)}$, $p_1={sprintf('%.2f', p1)}$",
      "{if_else(str_detect(label, 'base'), ' (base)', '')}"
    ),
    `N_init` = n_init,
    `z critical` = z_crit,
    `Exact critical` = exact_crit,
    `z T1E` = percent(z_t1e, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Exact T1E` = percent(exact_t1e, accuracy = 0.01),
    `z power` = percent(z_power, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Exact power` = percent(exact_power, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = Setting) |>
  cols_label(
    Setting = "Setting",
    `N_init` = md("$N_\\mathrm{init}$"),
    `z critical` = md("$c_z$"),
    `Exact critical` = md("$c_e$"),
    `z T1E` = md("$z$ T1E"),
    `Exact T1E` = "Exact T1E",
    `z power` = md("$z$ power"),
    `Exact power` = "Exact power"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(md(
    "One-sided $\\alpha=5\\%$. The exact test uses the smallest critical count whose null upper-tail probability is no greater than $\\alpha$."
  )) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), table.font.size = "scriptsize",
              heading.title.font.size = "small",
              heading.subtitle.font.size = "footnotesize")
```

```{r fig-generalizability}
#| fig-cap: "Exact CP-$z$ Type I error across five design configurations, with $\\text{CP}_U = 0.80$ and $\\text{CP}_\\text{fut} = 0.10$ held fixed, by exact enumeration. Each panel shows the setting-specific fixed-$N$ $z$-test Type I error (grey dashed) and nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$ (red dotted). The sign of the attained-level bias relative to $\\alpha$ changes across configurations, so the base-setting result is not universal."
#| fig-height: 7.2

# Data-driven vertical range. scale_y_continuous(limits = ...) DROPS points
# outside the range rather than zooming, which silently deletes any design
# setting whose exact T1E falls outside the window. coord_cartesian() zooms
# without discarding data, and the range is computed from gen_results so that
# adding or changing settings cannot clip the plot.
gen_rng  <- range(gen_results$power, na.rm = TRUE)
gen_pad  <- max((max(gen_rng[2], alpha) - min(gen_rng[1], alpha)) * 0.08, 2e-3)
gen_ylim <- c(min(gen_rng[1], alpha) - gen_pad,
              max(gen_rng[2], alpha) + gen_pad)

gen_fixed_refs <- gen_grid |>
  transmute(

    Reference = "Fixed-N z test"

gen_reference_lines <- bind_rows(
  gen_fixed_refs,
  gen_grid |>
    transmute(scenario_label = label, value = alpha,
              Reference = "Nominal alpha")
) |>
  mutate(Reference = factor(Reference,
                            levels = c("Nominal alpha", "Fixed-N z test")))

gen_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cp_lower, y = power)) +
  # Both references appear in every panel, so they are separated by colour as

  geom_hline(

  ) +
```
