```{r fig-generalizability}
  geom_point(color = COL_BLUE, size = 2.4, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ scenario_label,
    ncol = 2,
    labeller = labeller(
      scenario_label = as_labeller(gen_strip_labels, default = label_parsed)
    )
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Nominal alpha" = "dotted",
                                   "Fixed-N z test" = "dashed"),
                        name = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Nominal alpha"  = COL_ALPHA,
                                "Fixed-N z test" = COL_FIXED),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1),
                     breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = gen_ylim) +
  labs(
    x = TeX("CP promising lower bound ($\\textrm{CP}_L$)"),
    y = "Exact Type I error"
  ) +
  fig_theme(legend = "bottom") +
  theme(panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.1, "lines"))
```


The Bayesian PP design also varies across parameter settings. To mirror the
CP analysis, we sweep $\gamma_\mathrm{final}$ in each of the same five
configurations while holding the prior, interim efficacy threshold, and PP
zone boundaries fixed. The Type I error curve is a monotone step function
in every configuration. Because it is decreasing, any threshold at or above
the largest of the setting-specific smallest controlling values controls
the level everywhere, so a common conservative choice does exist. What does
not transfer is the *calibration*: the smallest controlling threshold, the
one that comes closest to spending the budget, differs by setting.

```{r pp-generalizability}
#| cache: true
gen_pp_results <- pmap_dfr(gen_grid, function(p0, p1, n_int, n_init, n_max, label) {
  map_dfr(gamma_fin_grid, function(gf) {
    bayes_oc_exact(
      p_true = p0, gamma_fin = gf,
      n_init = n_init, n_int = n_int, n_max = n_max,
      p0 = p0, ap = ap, bp = bp
    ) |>
      mutate(scenario_label = label, p0 = p0, p1 = p1)
  })
})
```

```{r pp-gen-summary}
#| include: false
# Smallest controlling gamma_final in each configuration; NA where none of the
# evaluated thresholds controls the level.
pp_gen_ctrl <- gen_pp_results |>
  filter(power <= alpha) |>
  group_by(scenario_label) |>
  slice_min(gamma_fin, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
pp_gen_n_ctrl <- nrow(pp_gen_ctrl)
pp_gen_n_set  <- dplyr::n_distinct(gen_pp_results$scenario_label)
```

The smallest controlling $\gamma_\mathrm{final}$ differs across
configurations, ranging from `r min(pp_gen_ctrl$gamma_fin)` to
`r max(pp_gen_ctrl$gamma_fin)` among the
`r pp_gen_n_ctrl` of `r pp_gen_n_set` settings in which any evaluated
threshold controls the level. A threshold of
`r max(pp_gen_ctrl$gamma_fin)` therefore controls Type I error in all of
them, but it is the least conservative choice in only one; elsewhere it
spends well under the budget and gives away power unnecessarily. Selecting
a threshold that both controls the level and comes close to spending it
requires enumeration in the design at hand. Supplementary Figure S1 shows
the full sweep in each setting.


## Final-Rule and Adaptation-Mapping Comparison {#sec-factorial}

We next retain the estimated-effect CP zone classification and its mapping
from each interim response count to final sample size, but replace the final
$z$-test rejection count with $c_e(N,\alpha)$. This evaluates whether the
exact final rule controls Type I error after the sample size has been
selected adaptively.

```{r tbl-exact-final}
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Exact operating characteristics after replacing only the final z-test rule with the exact one-sided binomial rule. The estimated-effect CP adaptation mapping is identical between columns."
exact_final_sweep <- map_dfr(cp_lower_grid, function(pl) {
  z0 <- cp_sweep |>
    filter(p_true == p0, round(cp_lower, 4) == round(pl, 4)) |>
    pull(power)
  z1 <- cp_sweep |>
    filter(p_true == p1, round(cp_lower, 4) == round(pl, 4)) |>
    pull(power)
  e0 <- cp_oc_exact_final(p0, pl, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE)$power
  e1 <- cp_oc_exact_final(p1, pl, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE)$power
  tibble(cp_lower = pl, z_t1e = z0, exact_t1e = e0,
         z_power = z1, exact_power = e1)
})

exact_final_sweep |>
  transmute(
    `CP_L` = sprintf("%.2f", cp_lower),
    `z T1E` = percent(z_t1e, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Exact T1E` = percent(exact_t1e, accuracy = 0.01),
    `z power` = percent(z_power, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Exact power` = percent(exact_power, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Power cost` = sprintf("%.2f pp", 100 * (z_power - exact_power))
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    `CP_L` = md("$\\mathrm{CP}_L$"),
    `z T1E` = md("$z$ T1E"),
    `Exact T1E` = "Exact T1E",
    `z power` = md("$z$ power"),
    `Exact power` = "Exact power",
    `Power cost` = "Power cost"
  ) |>
tab_source_note(md(glue(
  "Exact-final T1E ranges from ",
  "{percent(min(exact_final_sweep$exact_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)} to ",
  "{percent(max(exact_final_sweep$exact_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)} and remains ",
  "below {percent(alpha, accuracy = 1)} at every evaluated $\\mathrm{{CP}}_L$."
))) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), table.font.size = "small")
```

```{r fig-exact-final}
#| include: false
#| fig-cap: "Exact Type I error (left) and exact power at $p_1$ (right) after changing only the final decision rule. Both series use the identical estimated-effect CP adaptation mapping, so the vertical separation is attributable to the final rule alone. The red dotted line in the left panel is nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$. The exact binomial final controls the level at every $\\text{CP}_L$ on the grid, at a power cost quantified in the text."
#| fig-height: 4.5

exact_t1e_plot_data <- exact_final_sweep |>
  select(cp_lower, `z final` = z_t1e,
         `Exact binomial final` = exact_t1e) |>
  pivot_longer(-cp_lower, names_to = "Final rule", values_to = "value")

exact_power_plot_data <- exact_final_sweep |>
  select(cp_lower, `z final` = z_power,
         `Exact binomial final` = exact_power) |>
  pivot_longer(-cp_lower, names_to = "Final rule", values_to = "value")

exact_method_colors <- c(
  "z final" = COL_GOLD,
  "Exact binomial final" = COL_BLUE
)
exact_method_lines <- c(
  "z final" = "solid",
  "Exact binomial final" = "longdash"
)
exact_method_shapes <- c(
  "z final" = 16,
  "Exact binomial final" = 21
)

# Left panel uses a fixed 3%-6% axis at 0.5% intervals. Verify the series
# lies inside the window so a future parameter change cannot clip it silently.
ef_t1e_lim <- c(0.03, 0.06)
stopifnot(min(exact_t1e_plot_data$value) >= ef_t1e_lim[1],
          max(exact_t1e_plot_data$value) <= ef_t1e_lim[2])
ef_t1e_span <- diff(ef_t1e_lim)

p_exact_t1e <- exact_t1e_plot_data |>
  ggplot(aes(cp_lower, value, color = `Final rule`,
             linetype = `Final rule`, shape = `Final rule`)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, color = COL_ALPHA,
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_point(size = 2.7, stroke = 1.1, fill = "white") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.80, hjust = 1,
           y = ann_above(alpha, ef_t1e_span),
           label = TeX("$\\alpha = 5\\%$"),
           size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_ALPHA) +
  scale_color_manual(values = exact_method_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = exact_method_lines) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = exact_method_shapes) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1),
                     breaks = seq(0.03, 0.06, by = 0.005)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ef_t1e_lim) +
  labs(x = TeX("$\\textrm{CP}_L$"), y = "Exact Type I error") +
  fig_theme(legend = "bottom")

p_exact_power <- exact_power_plot_data |>
  ggplot(aes(cp_lower, value, color = `Final rule`,
             linetype = `Final rule`, shape = `Final rule`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_point(size = 2.7, stroke = 1.1, fill = "white") +
  scale_color_manual(values = exact_method_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = exact_method_lines) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = exact_method_shapes) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = TeX("$\\textrm{CP}_L$"), y = TeX("Exact power at $p_1$")) +
  fig_theme(legend = "bottom")

(p_exact_t1e + p_exact_power + plot_layout(guides = "collect")) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

The exact final controls on the full grid: T1E ranges from
`r percent(min(exact_final_sweep$exact_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(exact_final_sweep$exact_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`. At
$\text{CP}_L=0.50$, the exact-final design has
`r percent(exact_final_sweep |> filter(cp_lower == 0.50) |> pull(exact_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`
T1E and
`r percent(exact_final_sweep |> filter(cp_lower == 0.50) |> pull(exact_power), accuracy = 0.01)`
power, compared with
`r percent(exact_final_sweep |> filter(cp_lower == 0.50) |> pull(z_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`
and
`r percent(exact_final_sweep |> filter(cp_lower == 0.50) |> pull(z_power), accuracy = 0.01)`
for the $z$ final. Across the grid, the exact-final power cost ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(exact_final_sweep$z_power - exact_final_sweep$exact_power))`
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max(exact_final_sweep$z_power - exact_final_sweep$exact_power))`
percentage points. Supplementary Table S15 and Figure S4 give the full
grid.

To separate three distinct questions, we compare no adaptation,
CP-triggered adaptation, and PP-triggered adaptation under both the $z$ and
posterior final rules. Within each adaptive row, the mapping from interim
count to selected sample size is frozen when the final rule is swapped.
Interim efficacy stopping is disabled because it is itself a decision rule;
the design-specific futility rules remain part of each adaptive mapping. We
use $\text{CP}_L=0.50$ and the prospectively selected
$\gamma_\mathrm{final}=0.955$. The no-adaptation row evaluates each final
rule at $N_\mathrm{init}$ and supplies the reference needed to quantify the
effect of adapting.

```{r factorial-compute}
#| include: false
# Computes the factorial cells and contrasts used in the prose below and in
# @fig-factorial. The rendered table moved to the supplement (Table S3).
factorial_one <- function(p_true) {
  bind_rows(
    fixed_n_oc(p_true, n_init, p0, alpha, rule = "z",
               ap = ap, bp = bp, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected) |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "No adaptation", `Final rule` = "z test"),
    fixed_n_oc(p_true, n_init, p0, alpha, rule = "posterior",
               ap = ap, bp = bp, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected) |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "No adaptation", `Final rule` = "Posterior"),
    cp_oc_exact(p_true, 0.50, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "CP-triggered", `Final rule` = "z test"),
    cp_oc_post_final(p_true, 0.50, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected,
                     cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE) |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "CP-triggered", `Final rule` = "Posterior"),
    bayes_oc_ztest_final(p_true, gamma_int = Inf,
                         gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected,
                         pp_target = "posterior") |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "PP-triggered", `Final rule` = "z test"),
    bayes_oc_exact(p_true, gamma_fin_selected, gamma_int = Inf) |>
      mutate(Adaptation = "PP-triggered", `Final rule` = "Posterior")
  ) |>
    select(Adaptation, `Final rule`, power)
}

factorial_results <- factorial_one(p0) |>
  rename(t1e = power) |>
  left_join(factorial_one(p1) |> rename(power = power),
            by = c("Adaptation", "Final rule")) |>
  mutate(
    Adaptation = factor(
      Adaptation,
      levels = c("No adaptation", "CP-triggered", "PP-triggered")
    )
  )

adaptive_factorial <- factorial_results |>
  filter(Adaptation != "No adaptation")

adaptive_final_rule_contrast <- with(
  adaptive_factorial,
  mean(t1e[`Final rule` == "z test"]) -
    mean(t1e[`Final rule` == "Posterior"])
)
cp_pp_mapping_contrast <- with(
  adaptive_factorial,
  mean(t1e[Adaptation == "CP-triggered"]) -
    mean(t1e[Adaptation == "PP-triggered"])
)
fixed_final_rule_contrast <- with(
  factorial_results,
  t1e[Adaptation == "No adaptation" & `Final rule` == "z test"] -
    t1e[Adaptation == "No adaptation" & `Final rule` == "Posterior"]
)

no_adaptation_t1e <- factorial_results |>
  filter(Adaptation == "No adaptation") |>
  select(`Final rule`, fixed_t1e = t1e)
adaptation_deltas <- factorial_results |>
  filter(Adaptation != "No adaptation") |>
  left_join(no_adaptation_t1e, by = "Final rule") |>
  mutate(delta_t1e = t1e - fixed_t1e)

```

```{r factorial-power-summary}
#| include: false
fact_pow <- factorial_results |>
  select(Adaptation, `Final rule`, power) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = `Final rule`, values_from = power)

# Power gains of each adaptive cell over the no-adaptation cell using the
# SAME final rule, and the final-rule power contrast within the
# no-adaptation row. Computed because the prose compares the two.
.na_row <- fact_pow |> filter(Adaptation == "No adaptation")
fact_pow_gain <- fact_pow |>
  filter(Adaptation != "No adaptation") |>
  mutate(gain_z    = `z test`  - .na_row$`z test`,
         gain_post = Posterior - .na_row$Posterior) |>
  select(gain_z, gain_post) |>
  unlist() |>
  unname()
fact_pow_rule_contrast <- .na_row$`z test` - .na_row$Posterior
```

@fig-factorial shows Type I error. Power at $p_1$ is reported in
Supplementary Table S3. The $z$ rule is more powerful than the posterior
rule in every mapping, as it is at fixed $N$: within the no-adaptation row
the two give
`r percent(fact_pow$"z test"[fact_pow$Adaptation == "No adaptation"], accuracy = 0.01)`
and
`r percent(fact_pow$Posterior[fact_pow$Adaptation == "No adaptation"], accuracy = 0.01)`.
The across-row ordering does not match the Type I error ordering, however,
and the effect of adapting on power is not uniformly smaller than the
final-rule contrast: relative to the corresponding no-adaptation cell the
adaptive cells gain between
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(fact_pow_gain))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max(fact_pow_gain))` percentage points, the
largest of which exceeds the
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * fact_pow_rule_contrast)`-point final-rule
contrast in that row. Power comparisons across this table therefore have
to name the mapping as well as the rule.

```{r fig-factorial}
#| fig-cap: "Exact Type I error in the base setting for each combination of sample-size mapping and final decision rule. The no-adaptation row evaluates both final rules at the planned sample size and supplies the reference against which adaptation is judged. The two adaptive rows hold the interim-to-sample-size mapping fixed while swapping only the final rule, so the grey connecting segment within each row is the final-rule contrast for that mapping. The red dotted vertical line is nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$. Contrasts are quantified in the text; the CP-versus-PP row difference is a contrast between two adaptive mappings and is not the effect of adapting versus not adapting."
#| fig-height: 4.6

factorial_segments <- factorial_results |>
  group_by(Adaptation) |>
  summarise(x = min(t1e), xend = max(t1e), .groups = "drop")

comparison_rng <- range(c(factorial_results$t1e, alpha))
causal_pad <- max(diff(comparison_rng) * 0.12, 0.002)
causal_xlim <- comparison_rng + c(-causal_pad, causal_pad)

factorial_results |>
  ggplot(aes(t1e, Adaptation)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = alpha, color = COL_ALPHA,
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(
    data = factorial_segments,
    aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = Adaptation, yend = Adaptation),
    color = COL_FIXED, linewidth = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = `Final rule`, shape = `Final rule`),
             size = 3.4, stroke = 1.2, fill = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(t1e, accuracy = 0.01)),
            nudge_y = 0.19, size = FIG_ANN) +
  # The alpha reference is vertical here, so its label sits at the top of the
  # panel rather than above a horizontal line.
  annotate("text", x = alpha, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6, hjust = -0.08,
           label = TeX("$\\alpha = 5\\%$"),
           size = FIG_ANN, color = COL_ALPHA) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("z test" = COL_GOLD,
                                "Posterior" = COL_BLUE)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("z test" = 16, "Posterior" = 21)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = causal_xlim, clip = "off") +
  labs(
    x = "Exact Type I error", y = "Sample-size mapping",
    color = "Final rule", shape = "Final rule"
  ) +
  fig_theme(legend = "bottom") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

@fig-factorial and Supplementary Table S3 show that, within the two frozen
adaptive mappings, the average $z$-versus-posterior contrast is
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * adaptive_final_rule_contrast)` percentage points.
The `r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * cp_pp_mapping_contrast)`-point contrast is
instead the difference between CP- and PP-triggered mappings; it is not the
effect of SSR versus no SSR. Relative to the fixed-$N$ row, the complete
adaptive-design effects, including the design-specific futility rules, range from
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * min(adaptation_deltas$delta_t1e))` to
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * max(adaptation_deltas$delta_t1e))` points across
the four mapping/final-rule combinations. Thus the complete adaptation can
attenuate or increase T1E, and its contribution depends on both components. In this base
design, the fixed-$N$ final-rule contrast is
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * fixed_final_rule_contrast)` points, supporting a
narrow conclusion that final critical-count calibration is the larger
source of the observed difference here, not a universal causal ranking.

Because the descriptive contrasts depend on both tuning parameters, we
repeated the adaptive comparison across the full prespecified
$\text{CP}_L$ and $\gamma_\mathrm{final}$ grids.

```{r factorial-sensitivity-compute}
#| include: false
factorial_sensitivity <- expand_grid(
  cp_lower = cp_lower_grid,
  gamma_fin = gamma_fin_grid
) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(cp_lower, gamma_fin) {
    cp_z <- cp_oc_exact(
      p0, cp_lower, cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE
    )$power
    cp_post <- cp_oc_post_final(
      p0, cp_lower, gamma_fin = gamma_fin,
      cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE
    )$power
    pp_z <- bayes_oc_ztest_final(
      p0, gamma_int = Inf, gamma_fin = gamma_fin,
      pp_target = "posterior"
    )$power
    pp_post <- bayes_oc_exact(
      p0, gamma_fin, gamma_int = Inf
    )$power
    tibble(
      cp_lower = cp_lower,
      gamma_fin = gamma_fin,
      final_rule_contrast = ((cp_z + pp_z) - (cp_post + pp_post)) / 2,
      cp_pp_mapping_contrast = ((cp_z + cp_post) - (pp_z + pp_post)) / 2
    )
  })

# The ordering claimed in the text is a claim about MAGNITUDES. The signed
# comparison is close to vacuous here, because the final-rule contrast is
# bounded below by zero on this grid while the mapping contrast changes
# sign, so "larger" would hold almost automatically. Compare |.| instead,
# and separate the thresholds that actually control the level from the one
# that does not: gamma_fin_cal is by construction the smallest grid value
# with T1E <= alpha, so any smaller value is excluded by the prospective
# selection rule and is not a design anyone would field.
fs_mag <- factorial_sensitivity |>
  mutate(final_larger = abs(final_rule_contrast) >
                        abs(cp_pp_mapping_contrast))
fs_n_total       <- nrow(fs_mag)
fs_n_final_wins  <- sum(fs_mag$final_larger)
fs_exceptions    <- fs_mag |> filter(!final_larger)
fs_exc_gammas    <- sort(unique(fs_exceptions$gamma_fin))
fs_controlling   <- fs_mag |> filter(gamma_fin >= gamma_fin_cal)

# The prose states two things that must not drift: that every exception
# lies at a single gamma_final, and that there are none once the grid is
# restricted to level-controlling thresholds. Assert both.
stopifnot(
  length(fs_exc_gammas) == 1L,
  all(fs_controlling$final_larger)
)
```

Across the full $\text{CP}_L \times \gamma_\mathrm{final}$ grid the
final-rule contrast is the larger of the two in absolute value at
`r fs_n_final_wins` of the `r fs_n_total` combinations. The exceptions
occur only at $\gamma_\mathrm{final} =
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(fs_exc_gammas))`$, the one grid value at which the
two final rules very nearly coincide, so that the final-rule contrast
collapses toward zero while the mapping contrast does not. That value is
also the one the prospective calibration rule rejects, because its
attained level exceeds $\alpha$; restricted to the thresholds
that do control the level, $\gamma_\mathrm{final} \geq
`r gamma_fin_cal`$, the final-rule contrast is larger in absolute value at
every combination. The ordering reported above is therefore a property of
the level-controlling region of the grid rather than of one threshold
pair, but it is not a property of the grid as a whole. Supplementary
Table S4 gives the ranges.

The sensitivity ranges confirm that the numerical contrasts are
threshold-specific; they are descriptive evidence for the base design, not
invariant effects of either component.

```{r coherent-pp-z}
#| include: false
coherent_pp_z_t1e <- bayes_oc_ztest_final(
  p_true = p0, gamma_int = Inf, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected,
  pp_target = "ztest"
)$power
```

A coherent PP-$z$ design that recalculates PP against the $z$ boundary,
rather than freezing the posterior-target mapping, has
`r percent(coherent_pp_z_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error. It is reported
separately because both the adaptation mapping and final rule change.


## Combination-Test Comparator

The inverse-normal combination test retains the CP adaptation mapping but
uses stagewise binomial evidence. We choose the conventional planned
information-fraction weights
$w_1=\sqrt{n_1/N_0}$ and $w_2=\sqrt{1-n_1/N_0}$ before the trial and reject
when

$$w_1\Phi^{-1}(1-P_1)+w_2\Phi^{-1}(1-P_2)>z_{1-\alpha}.$$

The weights remain fixed when $N$ is re-estimated; only the sample size used
to construct $P_2$ changes. Conditional on stage 1 and the selected stage-2
size, the exact upper-tail $P_2$ is super-uniform, which gives the validity
argument stated in Section 2.2 [@lehmacher1999; @cui1999]. A futility stop is a nonrejection and no
combination statistic is computed. Otherwise, $P_2$ uses only post-interim
responses. Mid-$p$ values reduce conservatism but do not guarantee control
[@lancaster1961].

```{r tbl-combination}
#| tbl-cap: "Exact operating characteristics of the conventional z final and inverse-normal combination tests at $\\mathrm{CP}_L=0.50$. All three use the same observed-effect CP adaptation rule."
comb_results <- expand_grid(
  cp_lower = cp_lower_grid,
  p_true = c(p0, p1),
  pval = c("exact", "midp")
) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(cp_lower, p_true, pval) {
    comb_oc_exact(p_true, cp_lower, pval = pval,
                  cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE)
  })

comb_at_half <- comb_results |>
  filter(cp_lower == 0.50) |>
  mutate(Method = recode(pval, exact = "Exact combination",
                          midp = "Mid-p combination")) |>
  select(Method, p_true, power)

z_at_half <- cp_sweep |>
  filter(cp_lower == 0.50, p_true %in% c(p0, p1)) |>
  transmute(Method = "Final z test", p_true, power)

comb_half_values <- bind_rows(z_at_half, comb_at_half)
exact_comb_t1e <- comb_half_values |>
  filter(Method == "Exact combination", p_true == p0) |> pull(power)
exact_comb_power <- comb_half_values |>
  filter(Method == "Exact combination", p_true == p1) |> pull(power)
z_half_power <- comb_half_values |>
  filter(Method == "Final z test", p_true == p1) |> pull(power)
exact_comb_power_cost <- z_half_power - exact_comb_power

comb_half_values |>
  mutate(Estimand = if_else(p_true == p0, "Type I error", "Power"),
         Probability = percent(power, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  select(Method, Estimand, Probability) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Estimand, values_from = Probability) |>
  gt() |>
# Source notes are plain prose: Markdown math inside gt() source notes does
# not render reliably through the LaTeX pipeline and leaks the markup.
tab_source_note(glue(
  "Across the promising lower-bound grid, exact-combination Type I error is ",
  "{percent(min(comb_results$power[comb_results$p_true == p0 & comb_results$pval == 'exact']), accuracy = 0.01)}-",
  "{percent(max(comb_results$power[comb_results$p_true == p0 & comb_results$pval == 'exact']), accuracy = 0.01)}; ",
  "mid-p Type I error is ",
  "{percent(min(comb_results$power[comb_results$p_true == p0 & comb_results$pval == 'midp']), accuracy = 0.01)}-",
  "{percent(max(comb_results$power[comb_results$p_true == p0 & comb_results$pval == 'midp']), accuracy = 0.01)}."
)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels())
```

```{r midp-summary}
#| include: false

# Mid-p is not uniformly noncontrolling on this grid. Report where it does
# control, and at what power, rather than only its worst case: a reader who
# reads the table will see the favourable point regardless.
midp_t1e <- comb_results |>
  filter(p_true == p0, pval == "midp") |>
  select(cp_lower, t1e = power)
midp_pow <- comb_results |>
  filter(p_true == p1, pval == "midp") |>
  select(cp_lower, pow = power)
midp_join <- left_join(midp_t1e, midp_pow, by = "cp_lower")
midp_ok   <- midp_join |> filter(t1e <= alpha)
```

As @tbl-combination shows, at $\text{CP}_L=0.50$ the exact combination test
gives `r percent(exact_comb_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error and
`r percent(exact_comb_power, accuracy = 0.01)` power, a
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * exact_comb_power_cost)`-point power cost relative
to the final $z$ test.

The mid-$p$ variant is not uniformly noncontrolling, and we report its
behaviour in full rather than by its worst case alone. It controls at
`r nrow(midp_ok)` of `r nrow(midp_join)` grid points, attaining
`r percent(min(midp_join$t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` Type I error with
`r percent(midp_join$pow[which.min(midp_join$t1e)], accuracy = 0.01)`
power at $\text{CP}_L = `r midp_join$cp_lower[which.min(midp_join$t1e)]`$,
which is higher power than any exact route considered here. At the
remaining grid points it exceeds $\alpha$, reaching
`r percent(max(midp_join$t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`. Because mid-$p$
$p$-values are not super-uniform, this control is incidental to the
particular grid point rather than guaranteed, and it cannot be relied on
without exact verification of the specific design. That is precisely the
distinction the exact version removes: its validity follows from the
invariance argument and does not require checking.

The exact version therefore supplies a constructive binary implementation of
the fixed-weight combination-test framework discussed alongside promising-zone
SSR, with a quantifiable power cost. It is not the binary counterpart of the
Chen--DeMets--Lan argument for retaining a conventional final statistic.

## PP Boundary and Composite-Null Checks

The PP upper boundary determines how readily the trial increases its sample
size. We assessed values from 0.30 to 0.70 at the prospectively selected
final posterior threshold.

```{r pp-upper-compute}
#| include: false
pp_upper_results <- map_dfr(seq(0.30, 0.70, by = 0.10), function(pp_u) {
  bind_rows(
    bayes_oc_exact(p0, gamma_fin_selected, pp_upper = pp_u) |>
      mutate(Estimand = "Type I error"),
    bayes_oc_exact(p1, gamma_fin_selected, pp_upper = pp_u) |>
      mutate(Estimand = "Power")
  ) |> mutate(`PP upper` = pp_u)
})

pp_u_t1e <- pp_upper_results |> filter(Estimand == 'Type I error') |> pull(power)
pp_u_pow <- pp_upper_results |> filter(Estimand == 'Power') |> pull(power)
```

Varying $\mathrm{PP}_U$ from 0.30 to 0.70 at the selected final threshold
moves Type I error between
`r percent(min(pp_u_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` and
`r percent(max(pp_u_t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` and power between
`r percent(min(pp_u_pow), accuracy = 0.01)` and
`r percent(max(pp_u_pow), accuracy = 0.01)`. The boundary therefore has a
material efficiency effect but does not change the conclusion: Type I error
remains controlled across the range examined. Supplementary Table S5
reports the full sweep.

Finally, Supplementary Table S16 evaluates 201 equally spaced response rates
over the full composite null $[0, p_0]$. For every design shown the
rejection probability is nondecreasing in $p$ across the entire grid and
the largest value occurs at $p_0$, so the boundary is least favorable and
no interior maximum arises. This is a numerical result on a dense grid
rather than a monotonicity proof.

```{r tbl-least-favorable}
#| include: false
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical least-favorable-null check over 201 response rates at or below p0."
lfn <- list(
  "CP + z" = least_favorable_null(
    cp_oc_exact, p_null = p0, cp_lower = 0.50,
    cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE),
  "CP + exact binomial" = least_favorable_null(
    cp_oc_exact_final, p_null = p0, cp_lower = 0.50,
    cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE),
  "PP + posterior" = least_favorable_null(
    bayes_oc_exact, p_null = p0, gamma_fin = gamma_fin_selected),
  "Exact combination" = least_favorable_null(
    comb_oc_exact, p_null = p0, cp_lower = 0.50, pval = "exact",
    cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE),
  "Mid-p combination" = least_favorable_null(
    comb_oc_exact, p_null = p0, cp_lower = 0.50, pval = "midp",
    cp_mode = PRIMARY_CP_MODE)
)

lfn_summary <- imap_dfr(lfn, function(x, design) {
  # Monotonicity is reported, not asserted: check that the rejection
  # probability never decreases as p increases across the grid.
  tibble(Design = design, `Worst p` = x$p_worst,
         `Worst T1E` = x$t1e_worst,
         `At boundary` = if_else(x$at_boundary, "Yes", "No"),
         Monotone = if_else(min(diff(x$grid$t1e)) >= -1e-12, "Yes", "No"))
})

lfn_summary |>
  mutate(`Worst p` = sprintf("%.3f", `Worst p`),
         `Worst T1E` = percent(`Worst T1E`, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  gt() |>
  # Short column labels: the long forms ("Nondecreasing in p", "Maximum at
  # p0") pushed the table past the text width. Their meaning is given in the
  # source note instead.
  cols_label(
    `Worst p`     = md("$p^{*}$"),
    `Worst T1E`   = md("Max T1E"),
    `At boundary` = md("At $p_0$"),
    Monotone      = md("Monotone")
  ) |>
  # Plain prose: gt() source notes do not render Markdown math reliably
  # through the LaTeX pipeline.
  tab_source_note(
    paste("p* is the response rate maximising the rejection probability on",
          "the grid, and Max T1E is the value attained there. \"At p0\"",
          "indicates that the maximum falls at the null boundary;",
          "\"Monotone\" indicates that the rejection probability is",
          "nondecreasing across the whole grid, so no interior maximum",
          "arises.")
  ) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), table.font.size = "small")
```

## Interim-Timing Sensitivity

The base look occurs at 77% of planned information, so we repeated the
one-look analysis at target fractions of 40%, 50%, 65%, and 77%, corresponding
to $n_\text{int}=34$, 42, 55, and 65 after rounding to integer patient
counts. The planned and maximum sample sizes, zone boundaries, final rules,
and observed-effect CP projection remain fixed. For the PP design,
$\gamma_\text{final}$ is recalibrated prospectively at each timing by the
same smallest-controlling-grid-value rule used in the primary analysis.

```{r interim-timing-summary}
#| include: false

# Verify that the standalone timing script reproduces the existing base CP
# sweep exactly. This detects drift between the sensitivity implementation
# and the manuscript's primary analysis.
.timing_base <- interim_timing_cp |>
  filter(n_int == !!n_int) |>
  arrange(cp_lower)
.primary_base <- cp_sweep |>
  filter(abs(p_true - p0) < 1e-12) |>
  arrange(cp_lower)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(.timing_base$z_t1e, .primary_base$power,
                   tolerance = 1e-12))
)

timing_mapping_abs_max <- max(abs(interim_timing_cp$mapping_only_delta))
timing_final_delta_min <- min(interim_timing_cp$final_rule_delta)
timing_final_delta_max <- max(interim_timing_cp$final_rule_delta)
timing_half_t1e_range <- range(interim_timing_cp_summary$z_t1e)
timing_half_power_range <- range(interim_timing_cp_summary$z_power)
timing_pp_t1e_range <- range(interim_timing_pp_calibrated$t1e)
timing_pp_power_range <- range(interim_timing_pp_calibrated$power)
timing_pp_gamma <- interim_timing_pp_calibrated |>
  transmute(
    timing = timing_label,
    gamma = sprintf("%.3f", gamma_fin)
  )

timing_delta_plot <- interim_timing_cp_summary |>
  select(
    information_fraction,
    `Complete design` = total_adaptation_delta,
    `Mapping only` = mapping_only_delta,
    `Final rule` = final_rule_delta
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -information_fraction,
    names_to = "Contrast",
    values_to = "delta"
  )
```

@fig-interim-timing shows that timing materially changes the complete
operating design but not the ordering of the two mechanisms. At
$\text{CP}_L=0.50$, CP-$z$ Type I error ranges from
`r percent(min(timing_half_t1e_range), accuracy = 0.01)` at the earliest
look to `r percent(max(timing_half_t1e_range), accuracy = 0.01)` at the
latest, while power ranges from
`r percent(min(timing_half_power_range), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(timing_half_power_range), accuracy = 0.01)`. Across the
complete timing-by-$\text{CP}_L$ grid, however, the re-estimation mapping
with futility disabled changes Type I error by at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * timing_mapping_abs_max)` percentage points in
absolute value. Holding the CP mapping fixed and replacing the score-$z$
final by the exact-binomial final changes it by
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * timing_final_delta_min)` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * timing_final_delta_max)` points. The exact final
controls at every evaluated timing and $\text{CP}_L$.

```{r fig-interim-timing}
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity to the timing of the single interim look. Left: exact CP-$z$ Type I error across the promising-zone grid at four information fractions; the fixed-$N$ score-$z$ reference has no interim look. Right: signed Type I error contrasts at $\\text{CP}_L=0.50$. The complete-design contrast includes futility, the mapping-only contrast disables futility, and the final-rule contrast freezes the CP mapping while replacing the score-$z$ final with the exact-binomial final. All values are from exact enumeration."
#| fig-height: 4.8

timing_colors <- c(
  "40% (n=34)" = "#1B9E77",
  "50% (n=42)" = "#D95F02",
  "65% (n=55)" = "#7570B3",
  "77% (n=65)" = COL_FIXED
)

p_timing_grid <- interim_timing_cp |>
  ggplot(aes(cp_lower, z_t1e, color = timing_label,
             shape = timing_label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, color = COL_ALPHA,
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = headline_fixed_t1e, color = COL_FIXED,
             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.95) +
  geom_point(size = 2.3, stroke = 0.9, fill = "white") +
  scale_color_manual(values = timing_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18)) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
    shape = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(
    x = TeX("$\\textrm{CP}_L$"),
    y = "Exact Type I error",
    color = "Interim timing",
    shape = "Interim timing"
  ) +

timing_contrast_colors <- c(
  "Complete design" = COL_BLUE,
  "Mapping only" = COL_GOLD,
  "Final rule" = "#6A3D9A"
)

p_timing_delta <- timing_delta_plot |>
  ggplot(aes(information_fraction, 100 * delta,
             color = Contrast, shape = Contrast)) +

             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.6) +

    color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
    shape = "none"
  ) +

    breaks = interim_timing_grid$information_fraction,
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Interim information fraction",

    color = NULL,

  ) +

(p_timing_grid + p_timing_delta) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The prospectively calibrated PP design also changes with timing. The
smallest controlling $\gamma_\text{final}$ is
`r paste0(timing_pp_gamma$timing, ": ", timing_pp_gamma$gamma,
          collapse = "; ")`. Its exact Type I error ranges from
`r percent(min(timing_pp_t1e_range), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(timing_pp_t1e_range), accuracy = 0.01)`, with power from
`r percent(min(timing_pp_power_range), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(timing_pp_power_range), accuracy = 0.01)`. Thus an earlier
look does not invalidate the prospective calibration approach, but it can
change the selected threshold and operating efficiency. Supplementary
Tables S6 and S7 report the CP and PP timing results.


## Two-Look Sensitivity

We evaluated two prespecified two-look CP schedules, at 40%/65% and
50%/77% information. The design can stop for futility or retain or increase
its current target, but a later look cannot reverse an earlier increase.
There is no interim efficacy rejection, and the exact-final comparator
freezes the pathwise CP mapping.

```{r two-look-summary}
#| include: false

two_look_early <- two_look_cp_summary |> filter(n_look_1 == 34L)
two_look_late <- two_look_cp_summary |> filter(n_look_1 == 42L)
two_look_mapping_abs_max <- max(abs(two_look_cp_results$mapping_only_delta))
two_look_final_min <- min(two_look_cp_results$final_rule_delta)
two_look_final_max <- max(two_look_cp_results$final_rule_delta)
```

At $\text{CP}_L=0.50$, CP-$z$ Type I error is
`r percent(two_look_early$z_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` and
`r percent(two_look_late$z_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` in the two schedules, with
power `r percent(two_look_early$z_power, accuracy = 0.01)` and
`r percent(two_look_late$z_power, accuracy = 0.01)`. Across both schedules
and the full grid, the mapping-only contribution is at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * two_look_mapping_abs_max)` percentage points in
absolute value, versus `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * two_look_final_min)` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * two_look_final_max)` points for the final-rule
contrast; the frozen-mapping exact final controls throughout.

This bounded check is not a multiple-look theorem. Null futility is
`r percent(two_look_early$pr_fut_null, accuracy = 0.1)` and
`r percent(two_look_late$pr_fut_null, accuracy = 0.1)`, and designs with
three or more looks, interim efficacy, or repeated-look PP rules remain
outside scope. Supplementary Table S9 reports the full results.


## Practice-Oriented Sensitivity Analyses

Several checks align the evaluation more closely with prospective practice.
We repeated the CP analysis as a coherent
continuity-corrected score design: both conditional-power calculations and
the final rejection boundary use the correction. Across all four timings and
the full $\text{CP}_L$ grid, exact Type I error is
`r percent(min(continuity_corrected_timing$t1e), accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(max(continuity_corrected_timing$t1e), accuracy = 0.01)`, with
power of `r percent(min(continuity_corrected_timing$power), accuracy = 0.01)`
to `r percent(max(continuity_corrected_timing$power), accuracy = 0.01)`.
Thus continuity correction controls the level in the settings examined, but
every evaluated operating point misses the 80% target: the shortfall ranges
from `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (power - max(continuity_corrected_timing$power)))`
to `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (power - min(continuity_corrected_timing$power)))`
percentage points. This complete alternative therefore requires redesign to
recover power; it is not a ready replacement for the primary design.

On a 0.001 grid, the smallest controlling posterior threshold remains
$\gamma_\mathrm{final} = `r sprintf("%.3f", pp_fine_selected$gamma_fin)`$,
with exact Type I error
`r percent(pp_fine_selected$t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` and power
`r percent(pp_fine_selected$power, accuracy = 0.01)`. "Smallest controlling"
is grid-specific, not a continuous optimization result. Historical-control
drift is a recognized vulnerability of single-arm Phase II oncology designs
[@tang2010] and has a larger practical effect here: if the actual untreated rate is 0.25
while the design tests against $p_0=0.23$, positive-decision probabilities are
`r percent(historical_drift_results |> filter(abs(p_actual - 0.25) < 1e-12, Design == "CP + z") |> pull(positive_probability), accuracy = 0.01)`
for CP-$z$ and
`r percent(historical_drift_results |> filter(abs(p_actual - 0.25) < 1e-12, Design == "PP + posterior") |> pull(positive_probability), accuracy = 0.01)`
for PP-posterior. These are decision-risk probabilities, not Type I error
under the formal null. The unadjusted MLE has absolute bias at most
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(estimation_sensitivity$bias)))`; nominal 95%
Clopper--Pearson coverage [@clopper1934] ranges from
`r percent(min(estimation_sensitivity$exact_coverage), accuracy = 0.1)` to
`r percent(max(estimation_sensitivity$exact_coverage), accuracy = 0.1)`, and
Wilson coverage [@wilson1927] from
`r percent(min(estimation_sensitivity$wilson_coverage), accuracy = 0.1)` to
`r percent(max(estimation_sensitivity$wilson_coverage), accuracy = 0.1)`.
These are descriptive diagnostics, not adaptive-adjusted inference
[@fda2019; @shan2017].
Supplementary Tables S8, S10, and S11 and Figure S3 report the details.

# Discussion

**Interpretation.** In the base design the dominant contrast is between
final decision rules, not between adapting and not adapting. At fixed $N$,
replacing the posterior critical count with the score-$z$ count changes the
attained level by `r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * fixed_final_rule_contrast)`
percentage points. The isolated mapping contribution is at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * timing_mapping_abs_max)` points across one-look
timings from 40% to 77% information and remains smaller than the final-rule
contrast in the two evaluated two-look schedules. These are bounded
robustness checks, not a general ordering: the complete adaptive cells can
either attenuate or amplify the inherited level, and the CP-versus-PP
contrast compares two mappings rather than adaptation with no adaptation.

The mechanism is approximation error rather than discreteness. Exact,
posterior, and score rules all reduce to integer rejection counts, but over
the reachable sample sizes the uncorrected score-$z$ count is never larger
than the exact count and is often smaller. That relation is verified for
this design, not proved generally. The design-fixed inverse-normal
combination test instead obtains validity from super-uniform stagewise
$p$-values [@lehmacher1999; @cui1999].

**Calibration and alternatives.** $\text{CP}_L$ alone does not control the
base design when the other thresholds and nominal final level remain fixed.
Jointly recalibrating the final level and its CP mapping does produce a
controlling frequentist design. Likewise, the posterior design can be
calibrated prospectively through the monotone step function in
$\gamma_\mathrm{final}$, but its futility and favorable boundaries remain
part of the calibrated design. The finer grid selects the same posterior
threshold as the primary analysis; that value is grid-optimal under the
stated rule, not a continuous optimum.

Exact-binomial final and combination-test alternatives control Type I error
but are conservative in the reported operating points. Mid-$p$ values
recover power without the same guarantee. The coherent
continuity-corrected design also controls, but misses the 80% power target at
every timing examined. None of these methods was optimized under a common
power, expected-sample-size, or maximum-sample-size constraint, so the
results compare specified operating points rather than an efficiency
frontier. The factorial ordering is also conditional on the selected
posterior threshold and excludes interim efficacy stopping.

**Regulatory implication.** FDA guidance calls for demonstration of Type I
error control analytically where possible and otherwise by simulation
[@fda2019]. Exact enumeration is available here; more complex designs may
require validated simulation. Either route must evaluate the complete
prespecified adaptation and decision rule. The exact calculations are
cross-checked by a seeded simulation and by an independent base-R
implementation that reproduces six selected operating characteristics.

**Limitations.** The study concerns a one-sample binary endpoint, selected
design grids, a Jeffreys prior, one interim look at four timings, and two
prespecified two-look CP schedules. The full fixed-$N$/CP/PP comparison is
performed only in the base design; five additional configurations establish
heterogeneity but are not exhaustive. The least-favorable-null check is
numerical rather than a proof. Additional looks, delayed outcomes, and
multivariate endpoints may require recursive enumeration or validated
simulation. The exact procedures were not optimized or compared with
randomized exact tests [@lancaster1961], so their power costs are not lower bounds for all
exact frequentist methods.

*Interim timing.* The base look occurs at information fraction
`r sprintf("%.2f", headline_info_frac)`. The 40%--77% timing grid and two
two-look schedules preserve the reported ordering, but timing materially
changes zone occupancy, expected sample size, power, and PP calibration.
Looks before 40%, data-dependent timing, three or more looks, repeated PP
analyses, and interim efficacy in the two-look design remain unexamined; high
null futility further limits the two-look result.

*Projection and futility.* Primary CP uses the observed interim rate. The
design-alternative convention can change both the size and direction of the
SSR contribution. Moreover, statements about a small mapping effect disable
futility to isolate re-estimation; complete adaptive designs bundle these
components, and that bundled effect is not separately identified outside the
base setting.

*Posterior versus exact control.* At sample sizes reached by the PP mapping,
the selected posterior and exact-binomial boundaries can disagree. Freezing
the mapping and replacing the posterior boundary lowers Type I error from
`r percent(pp_post_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)` to
`r percent(pp_exact_t1e, accuracy = 0.01)`; posterior control is therefore a
property of the calibrated PP design, not another description of the exact
test.

*Historical controls and estimation.* The hypothesis treats $p_0$ as fixed.
Historical drift can dominate the calibration effects studied here, and the
sensitivity analysis cannot correct that bias [@tang2010]. The reported
ordinary Clopper--Pearson and Wilson intervals are post-adaptation
diagnostics, not adaptive-adjusted confidence procedures
[@fda2019; @shan2017].

*Operational deviations.* Enumeration assumes complete outcomes at the
prespecified looks, exact adherence to the rule, and no enrollment overrun.
Delayed or missing outcomes, misclassification, overrunning recruitment, and
unplanned look timing require separate evaluation [@fda2019].


# Conclusion

In the base design, the fixed score-$z$ test is already anticonservative,
and CP adaptation attenuates rather than creates that excess. The isolated
mapping contribution is smaller than the score-$z$ versus exact-final
contrast across the evaluated one- and two-look checks, but its sign and
magnitude remain design-specific.

Exact stagewise binomial $p$-values with fixed inverse-normal weights provide
a valid, conservative combination test. Replacing only the final rule with
an exact binomial test also controls throughout the evaluated grid, at a
power cost of
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * min(exact_final_sweep$z_power - exact_final_sweep$exact_power))`
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max(exact_final_sweep$z_power - exact_final_sweep$exact_power))`
points. Posterior and directly calibrated frequentist boundaries provide
other options; the coherent continuity-corrected design controls but misses
the 80% power target throughout. Whatever the rule, the complete adaptive
design must be prespecified and its operating characteristics verified
exactly or by validated simulation [@fda2019]. Valid testing alone does not resolve
historical-control validity or post-adaptation inference.


# Code and Data Availability

The analysis code is available in an anonymous R/Quarto repository at
<https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CP-SSR-Binary-Trials-8DB8/>. The non-anonymized public repository will be
disclosed after acceptance. The repository
contains the article and supplement sources, design constants, analysis
functions, sensitivity scripts, regression checks, and anonymization utility.
No external data are used. Every reported operating characteristic is
computed by exact enumeration, using the one-look engine or the repeated-look
recursion. A seeded Monte Carlo run is the sole stochastic element; it is a
shared-helper validation check and supplies no reported operating
characteristic. A separate base-R implementation shares neither decision
helpers nor parameter sources with the manuscript engine and reproduces six
selected fixed and adaptive results.

The documents require R $\geq$ 4.4 and the packages listed in the repository
README. Render the article before the supplement because the article writes
the exact result objects consumed by the supplementary source. Complete
reproduction instructions and a script-by-script inventory are provided in
the README.
